words.d: twisted and knotted, as with old branches, hands or roots
words.ex: The old fisherman mended nets with gnarled fingers.
words.ety: A word that sounds like what it means — try saying it slowly and picture a knotty old tree trunk.

words.d: a person hired to do many different kinds of jobs; a jack of all trades
words.ex: Our office factotum handles billing, the phones and even the coffee machine.
words.ety: Latin fac (make, do — think factory) + totum (all, as in total): someone who 'does it all'. Picture Batman's butler, Alfred.

words.d: forcing conformity by arbitrary, ruthless or violent means
words.ex: The procrustean dress code ignored every reasonable exception.
words.ety: From Procrustes, a mythical bandit who made travelers fit his iron bed — stretching the short ones and cutting off the feet of the tall ones. A 'procrustean bed' is an arbitrary standard everything must fit.

words.d: to destroy or kill a large part of something
words.ex: The drought decimated the region's wheat harvest.
words.hook: A giant die rolls through town with all its might, flattening buildings.
words.ety: Latin dec (ten, as in decade, decimal, decathlon). Roman commanders punished mutinous troops by executing one soldier in ten; the meaning later widened to 'destroy utterly'.

words.d: a commotion or fuss, usually over a minor disagreement
words.ex: There was a brief kerfuffle over who had reserved the table.
words.ety: Learn it alongside its meaning-cousins: spat and tussle (mild), hullabaloo (noisy), imbroglio (tangled), melee and donnybrook (violent free-for-alls).

words.d: organizing words into groups that share a meaning, to make them easier to remember and retrieve
words.ex: Instead of an A-to-Z list, she studied words for 'fight' together — that's semantic chunking.
words.ety: From Greek sēma (sign, meaning). Our brains store knowledge in 'schemas' — mental file folders — so grouping by meaning matches how memory works.

words.d: the history of a word: its origin and how its form and meaning have changed
words.ex: The etymology of 'decimate' involves Roman army discipline.
words.ety: Greek etymon (true sense) + -logy (study). An 'etymological narrative' is a story about a word's history — stories are easy to remember.

words.d: the study of the structure of words and their meaningful parts (prefixes, suffixes, roots)
words.ex: Morphology tells us that 'unbreakable' has three meaningful parts.
words.ety: Greek morph (form, shape) + -logy (study). Meaningful word parts are called morphemes.

words.d: artificial, not natural; or made-up and fake, a sham
words.ex: Her factitious laugh fooled no one at the table.
words.ety: Latin fac (make): things made by people in a factory are not natural. Don't confuse it with 'facetious' (joking, not serious).

words.d: joking or flippant, especially at an inappropriate time
words.ex: He was being facetious when he offered to sell his brother.
words.ety: Usage alert: often confused with factitious (artificial). Facetious = playful; factitious = fake.

words.d: cautious and careful, considering all risks before acting
words.ex: Be circumspect about what you post online.
words.ety: Latin circum (around) + spect (look): a careful person looks around before acting.

words.d: the words you understand when you read or hear them
words.ex: Your receptive vocabulary is much larger than the words you actually use.
words.ety: Compare 'expressive vocabulary': the words you can use comfortably in speech and writing.

words.d: a language's spelling system
words.ex: English orthography represents meaning as well as sound.
words.ety: Greek ortho (straight, correct) + graph (write): 'correct writing'.

words.d: a word part attached to a base or root — a prefix (front) or suffix (end)
words.ex: In 'unprofitable', un- and -able are affixes on the base word profit.
words.ety: Latin ad (to) + fix (fasten). A root (like spect) can't stand alone; a base word (like profit) can.

words.d: a flamboyant swindler who poses as an expert, especially one selling fake remedies
words.ex: The mountebank sold bottles of colored water as a cure for baldness.
words.ety: Italian 'monta in banco' — mount a bench: quacks climbed onto a bench in the town square to sell potions. Synonyms: charlatan, flimflammer, con artist.

words.d: someone who uses clever but deliberately misleading arguments
words.ex: The debate coach warned against becoming a sophist who wins without being right.
words.ety: Greek soph (wise, clever). Ancient Sophists taught persuasion and were accused of caring about winning, not truth. Sophistry = such trickery. Compare sophomore, 'wise fool'.

words.d: seeming plausible on the surface but actually false — and intended to mislead
words.ex: His specious argument fell apart under questioning.
words.ety: Latin speciosus (good-looking), from species (appearance) and spec (look). A specious claim looks good but isn't.

words.d: false or not genuine — not necessarily meant to deceive
words.ex: The study found a spurious link between shoe size and intelligence.
words.ety: Difference from specious: specious implies deliberate deception; spurious can just be wrong or an honest mistake. Common pairs: spurious charges, spurious reasoning.

words.d: of doubtful authenticity; widely told but probably untrue and unverifiable
words.ex: The tale of alligators in the sewers is apocryphal.
words.ety: From the Apocrypha, texts left out of the Bible because their authenticity couldn't be established. Think urban legends.

words.d: being an inferior or artificial substitute
words.ex: We drank ersatz coffee made from roasted chicory.
words.ety: German for 'substitute'. British prisoners in WWII were fed Ersatzbrot — bread bulked out with sawdust — and brought the word home.

words.d: underhanded, dishonest or deceitful behavior
words.ex: The election was marred by bribes, wiretaps and other skulduggery.
words.ety: Of Scottish origin; nothing to do with digging up skulls — but that grisly image can help you remember 'shady dealings'.

words.d: crafty schemes or secret plots
words.ex: The novel follows the political machinations of a royal court.
words.ety: Link mach- to Machiavelli, author of The Prince, the classic portrait of scheming rulers. Most common pairing: political machinations.

words.d: to swindle, cheat or trick
words.ex: We got hornswoggled into paying double for the tickets.
words.ety: An 1800s Americanism of unknown origin. A colorful (probably apocryphal) story: a lassoed cow wriggles its head to slip its horns free and cheat the cowboy. Cousins: bamboozle, hoodwink.

words.d: a persistently annoying person who keeps questioning, criticizing and pestering
words.ex: The local gadfly turned up at every council meeting with a new complaint.
words.ety: Literally a fly that bites livestock; Old Norse gaddr = spike, sting. Socrates called himself the gadfly that stung lazy Athens awake. Common pair: political gadfly.

words.d: complaining in a whining, peevish way
words.ex: The querulous passenger grumbled about the seat, the food and the pilot.
words.ety: Latin queri (to complain), the source of quarrel — not related to query. Picture Oscar the Grouch. Cousins: peevish (petty complaints), petulant (childish sulks), carp (nasty nitpicking).

words.d: tearfully and foolishly sentimental, often from drinking too much
words.ex: After a few drinks he got maudlin about his school days.
words.ety: From Mary Magdalene, painted in the Middle Ages as a weeping penitent. Picture a crying drunk spilling his life story.

words.d: excessively and sickeningly sentimental, often insincerely so
words.ex: The mawkish tribute from his rival made the audience cringe.
words.ety: Middle English mawke = maggot — think 'disgusting'. Maudlin = too emotional from lack of restraint; mawkish = sickening, fake sentiment.

words.d: cloying, sickly sweet sentiment or speech; also, molasses or golden syrup
words.ex: The greeting card was pure treacle.
words.ety: Picture thick, sticky syrup. Adjective: treacly. Related: cloying (overly sweet, ingratiating), saccharine.

words.d: indecent, salacious or scandalous; also, rough and scaly
words.ex: The tabloid printed every scabrous detail of the affair.
words.ety: Latin scaber (rough, scaly), from scabere (to scratch) — the family of scab and scabies. Rough skin → rough, shocking content.

words.d: offensive and disgusting, especially of smells; also harmful
words.ex: A noisome odor drifted from the forgotten lunchbox.
words.ety: Related to annoy, not to noise. (Noise comes from Latin nausea, 'seasickness', from Greek naus, ship.)

words.d: traditionally: excessive and insincere (fulsome flattery); now often: abundant, generous
words.ex: She received fulsome praise from the committee.
words.ety: A 'skunked term': it has shifted from 'abundant' to 'overfed' to 'offensively overdone' and back to 'abundant'. Because readers disagree, use it with care.

words.d: a pest who is both annoying and boring
words.ex: The neighborhood nudnik cornered me for an hour about lawn mowers.
words.ety: Borrowed from Yiddish. A gadfly who is also dull.

words.d: a wild free-for-all brawl; also a heated public dispute
words.ex: A shove between two players turned into a bench-clearing donnybrook.
words.ety: Donnybrook, a Dublin suburb whose annual fair was famous for drunken brawls — it was banned in 1855.

words.d: a complicated, confused and often embarrassing situation or dispute
words.ex: The love-triangle imbroglio was worthy of a sitcom.
words.ety: Pronounced im-BROHL-yo (silent g). Italian 'to confuse'; related to embroiled — and to broil and broth: picture everything jumbled in a boiling pot.

words.d: aggressively hostile; eager to fight
words.ex: The general's bellicose speech alarmed the neighboring countries.
words.ety: Latin bellum (war); keyword rebellion. Belligerent is a close cousin. Antebellum = before the war; postbellum = after.

words.d: fierce, cruel and eager to fight; also scathingly harsh (of criticism)
words.ex: The critic's truculent review called the novel a waste of paper.
words.ety: Unrelated to trucks — but picture an aggressive truck driver riding your bumper, and you won't forget it.

words.d: stubbornly disobedient to authority; willfully defiant
words.ex: The contumacious witness was held in contempt of court.
words.ety: Connect it to someone you know who thumbs their nose at rules.

words.d: aggressively and excessively greedy; predatory
words.ex: A rapacious developer bought up the whole waterfront.
words.ety: Emphasizes greedy, devouring aggression. Cousins: ravenous, voracious, avaricious.

words.d: calm, peaceful and happy (usually of a past time)
words.ex: She remembered the halcyon days of childhood summers.
words.ety: Greek myth: Alcyone became the halcyon (kingfisher); her father, god of the winds, calmed the sea so she could nest. Note the 'c' (sea) — picture a bird on a still sea.

words.d: quiet, still and at rest; also inactive or dormant
words.ex: After midnight the house settled into quiescence.
words.hook: Actors freeze, pretending to sleep, in a quiet scene so the mummies won't catch them.
words.ety: Latin quiescere (to rest), the family of quiet. Noun: quiescence.

words.d: to win back someone's favor; to appease
words.ex: He tried to propitiate his boss with an early report.
words.ety: Often religious (propitiating the gods). Synonyms: mollify, placate, conciliate, dulcify.

words.d: to pamper or overprotect someone excessively
words.ex: Stop mollycoddling him — he can make his own bed.
words.ety: Coddle = to pamper; 'molly' was once a mocking term for a pampered man.

words.d: to criticize or punish severely
words.ex: The coach castigated the team for their lazy defense.
words.ety: Word-part trick: you cast (throw) criticism at someone.

words.d: delicious; also (informally) attractive
words.ex: The bakery's toothsome pastries sell out by nine.
words.ety: 1550s: tooth (appetite, as in 'sweet tooth') + -some (causing). Something toothsome makes your teeth want it.

words.d: fault-finding; quick to object to trivial errors
words.ex: His captious boss never said a single kind word.
words.ety: Synonyms: hypercritical, carping, cantankerous. Non-example: someone encouraging and complimentary.

words.d: roundabout, evasive or wordy speech
words.ex: Cut the circumlocution and tell me what happened.
words.ety: Latin circum (around) + loc (speak): talking around the point. Picture the word written in a circle.

words.d: intended to help memory; a memory aid
words.ex: 'Roy G. Biv' is a mnemonic for the colors of the rainbow.
words.ety: From Mnemosyne, Greek goddess of memory. The 'm' is silent: ni-MON-ik.

words.d: a person who does evil or breaks the law
words.ex: The malefactors were caught on camera.
words.ety: Latin mal (bad) + fac (do): one who does bad things. Opposite: benefactor.

words.d: a curse; evil talk about someone
words.ex: The witch muttered a malediction as she left the village.
words.ety: mal (evil) + dict (speak) = evil speech. Antonym: benediction, a blessing.

words.d: a chronically dissatisfied person; also a political rebel
words.ex: The office malcontent complained even about free pizza.
words.ety: mal + content: 'badly contented'. A malcontent kvetches (Yiddish: to gripe, literally to squeeze).

words.d: a vague feeling of discomfort, unease or illness
words.ex: A general malaise settled over the team after the loss.
words.ety: mal + aise (ease): being ill at ease. Common phrase: economic malaise.

words.d: clumsy, awkward or tactless
words.ex: His maladroit attempt at a joke offended everyone.
words.ety: mal + adroit (skillful, agile).

words.d: wrongdoing, especially by a public official
words.ex: The mayor was removed from office for malfeasance.
words.ety: mal + Old French faisance (doing) — the same 'do' idea as fac.

words.d: to fake or exaggerate illness to avoid work or duty
words.ex: He malingered every Monday morning.
words.ety: Via French malingre (sickly). Picture a child warming the thermometer on a light bulb.

words.d: open to bribery; willing to sell one's influence
words.ex: A venal official waved the trucks through for cash.
words.ety: Latin venum (for sale), as in vendor and vending machine. Don't confuse with venial (minor, forgivable).

words.d: minor and forgivable (of a sin or fault)
words.ex: Forgetting to call back is a venial offense.
words.ety: Usage alert: venial = pardonable; venal = corruptible.

words.d: proceeding secretly and subtly, with harmful effects; treacherous
words.ex: High blood pressure is an insidious disease.
words.ety: Latin insidere (to sit in, lie in wait). Spelling hook: it works from the INSIDE.

words.d: likely to cause resentment or envy; unfairly discriminating
words.ex: The invidious remarks divided the audience.
words.ety: Latin invidia (envy). Spelling hook: iNViDious → eNVy.

words.d: depravity; shameful wickedness
words.ex: He was dismissed for moral turpitude.
words.ety: Latin turpis (shameful, ugly). Usually heard as 'moral turpitude'.

words.d: a shrewd, unprincipled person (often a politician)
words.ex: Only a snollygoster would promise one thing and vote for the opposite.
words.ety: An old Americanism — few people know it, so it's a safe insult.

words.d: just coming into existence and beginning to develop
words.ex: She led a nascent startup with big potential.
words.ety: Latin nasci (to be born); root nasc/nat as in nativity, natal, native. Synonyms: incipient, burgeoning, embryonic, fledgling.

words.d: just begun and not yet fully formed; disorganized
words.ex: His plan was still inchoate, so investors waited.
words.ety: Pronounced in-KOH-it. Compared with nascent, it highlights what is still lacking.

words.d: young and inexperienced; immature
words.ex: As a callow youth of nineteen, he struck out three times in his first game.
words.ety: Old English calu (bald, bare) — used of young birds without feathers. Memory hook: a callow person has a shallow pool of experience. Common phrase: callow youth.

words.d: a dabbler in an art or subject, often one who pretends to more knowledge than they have
words.ex: He's a dilettante who buys new gear for every hobby and masters none.
words.ety: Italian 'lover of the arts' (1700s); it turned negative by the late 1700s. Related: poser, pretender.

words.d: a beginner or novice
words.ex: Even a fly-fishing tyro like me caught a trout with a good guide.
words.ety: Synonyms: novice, rookie, neophyte, greenhorn, tenderfoot, abecedarian (someone learning the ABCs). Unlike dilettante, tyro carries no hint of pretending.

words.d: an innocent, naive young woman, or an actress who plays that stock role
words.ex: The ingenue arrived in the big city with stars in her eyes.
words.ety: From French ingénu (naive, ingenuous).

words.d: childishly silly and immature
words.ex: The investors' puerile jokes embarrassed the waiter.
words.ety: Latin puer (boy, child). Often used disapprovingly of adults' behavior.

words.d: near death; or no longer active and in decline
words.ex: The moribund downtown came back to life with new cafés.
words.ety: Latin mori (to die); root mort (death) as in mortal, mortuary, postmortem, mortify.

words.d: a person who is new to a subject, skill or belief
words.ex: The class is designed for neophytes with no coding experience.
words.ety: Greek neo (new) + phyt (planted): 'newly planted'.

words.d: unreasonable fear or hatred of foreigners or strangers
words.ex: The editorial warned against the rising xenophobia.
words.ety: Greek xeno (strange, foreign) + phobia (fear). A strange-sounding word for fear of strangers.

words.d: an abnormal fear of open or public spaces
words.ex: Her agoraphobia made crowded markets unbearable.
words.ety: Greek agora: the open marketplace and assembly area at the center of a Greek city.

words.d: fear of public speaking
words.ex: Glossophobia had his shirt soaked with sweat before the talk.
words.ety: Greek glossa (tongue). Keyword: polyglot, a speaker of many tongues.

words.d: an abnormal fear of heights
words.ex: My acrophobia keeps me well back from the cliff edge.
words.ety: Greek akros (top, height). Acrobats fly high; the Acropolis is the high city.

words.d: a supposed cure for all problems or diseases
words.ex: Technology is not a panacea for bad teaching.
words.ety: Greek pan (all) + akos (cure).

words.d: a complete or impressive collection or display
words.ex: The book covers the full panoply of human emotions.
words.ety: Greek pan (all) + hopla (arms): originally a full suit of armor.

words.d: a connoisseur or lover of wine
words.ex: The oenophile swirled his glass and spoke of blackberry notes.
words.ety: Greek oinos (wine) + phil (love). Pronounced EE-nuh-file.

words.d: a person who collects or studies stamps
words.ex: Any philatelist would dream of owning the one-cent British Guiana stamp.
words.ety: Greek phil (love) + ateleia (exemption from tax — a stamp showed postage was prepaid).

words.d: to kiss and cuddle; also to coax or wheedle
words.ex: A couple was canoodling in the back row of the cinema.
words.ety: 1850s American slang of uncertain origin. A fun (probably apocryphal) story: canoe + paddle, for couples escaping their chaperone.

words.d: a person who dislikes and distrusts humankind
words.ex: The old misanthrope only came to town twice a year.
words.ety: Greek miso (hate) + anthropos (human). Related: misanthropy, misogyny (hatred of women), misandry (hatred of men).

words.d: to denounce bitterly; to loathe intensely
words.ex: The crowd execrated the acquitted man as a thief.
words.ety: Latin ex (out, away) + sacrare (make sacred): to take the sacred away — leaving a curse. Adjective: execrable (detestable).

words.d: something or someone intensely disliked or loathed
words.ex: Small talk is anathema to a misanthrope.
words.ety: Originally a formal church curse; verb: anathematize, to denounce solemnly.

words.d: lacking flavor; lacking interest or excitement
words.ex: The roast was overcooked and insipid.
words.hook: A baby sips from a sippy cup and spits out the flavorless juice.
words.ety: Hook: sip a bland, tasteless drink. Stresses a lack of taste or interest.

words.d: lacking life, zest or spirit; dull and empty
words.ex: After forty years, his lectures had become vapid.
words.ety: Latin vapidus — that has lost its vapor, like a flat drink. Related word: vapor.

words.d: matter-of-fact and unimaginative; or commonplace and ordinary
words.ex: The manual was written in a prosaic, just-the-facts style.
words.ety: From prose (as opposed to imaginative poetry).

words.d: daily; ordinary and everyday
words.ex: Doing dishes and paying bills are quotidian chores.
words.ety: Latin quotidie (every day); -dian from dies (day), as in diurnal (daytime). Synonyms: routine, garden-variety.

words.d: the common people; the masses
words.ex: The heiress chartered private jets to avoid the hoi polloi.
words.ety: Greek 'the many'; polloi is related to poly (many) as in polygon. Not to be confused with hoity-toity.

words.d: so lacking in originality as to be boring; trite
words.ex: He could only manage banal remarks about the weather.
words.hook: An owl tosses away a bone because it's too plain and ordinary.
words.ety: Synonyms: trite, stale, threadbare, hackneyed (from a 'hack', a writer for hire who reuses tired phrases).

words.d: a trite, overused saying meant to soothe; a platitude
words.ex: The coach offered the usual bromides about giving 110%.
words.ety: Originally a sedative made with bromine — a bromide dulls your senses.

words.d: an aristocrat; having refined, upper-class manners and tastes
words.ex: Her patrician tastes ran to opera and fine dining.
words.ety: Latin pater (father): the founding families of Rome. Opposite: plebeian (common, lower class).

words.d: having no equal; unrivaled
words.ex: Messi is a dribbler nonpareil.
words.ety: French non (not) + pareil (equal). Often placed after the noun: 'a writer nonpareil'.

words.d: overused and therefore unoriginal and dull
words.ex: The film was full of hackneyed phrases.
words.ety: From hackney, a horse for hire — then a hired 'hack' writer.

words.d: endlessly laborious and futile
words.ex: Keeping up with my inbox is a Sisyphean task.
words.ety: King Sisyphus cheated death twice; the gods sentenced him to push a boulder up a hill forever — it always rolled back down just before the top.

words.d: requiring tremendous strength or effort
words.ex: Rebuilding the city was a Herculean job.
words.ety: From the hero Hercules and his twelve labors. Herculean stresses huge effort; Sisyphean stresses endless futility.

words.d: a constant, looming threat; an impending disaster
words.ex: The layoffs hung over the office like a sword of Damocles.
words.ety: The flatterer Damocles envied King Dionysius, so the king let him rule for a day — beneath a sword hanging by a single horsehair. Power brings constant fear.

words.d: an extremely complicated, seemingly unsolvable problem; 'to cut the Gordian knot' = to solve it with bold, decisive action
words.ex: The new manager cut the Gordian knot by scrapping the old system entirely.
words.ety: King Gordius tied an impossible knot; whoever undid it would rule Asia. Alexander the Great simply sliced through it with his sword.

words.d: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood; also lively and quick-witted
words.ex: Her mercurial temper kept everyone on edge.
words.ety: From Mercury (Greek Hermes), the swift, tricky messenger god — and the liquid metal quicksilver that never holds its shape.

words.d: a wild celebration of unrestrained revelry
words.ex: The victory party turned into a saturnalia that lasted until dawn.
words.ety: Saturnalia, Rome's December festival for Saturn, with feasting, gambling, gifts and masters serving slaves.

words.d: gloomy, sullen and brooding
words.ex: The saturnine poet rarely smiled.
words.ety: Astrologers believed people born under slow, cold, distant Saturn were gloomy. Synonyms: morose, glum, dour, sullen.

words.d: daringly original, creative and boldly inventive
words.ex: Einstein's Promethean ideas changed how we see the universe.
words.ety: Prometheus ('forethought') shaped humans from clay and stole fire from the gods to give them — and was chained to a mountain as punishment.

words.d: behaving as if one is superior; haughtily disdainful
words.ex: The supercilious maître d' looked me up and down.
words.hook: A haughty superintendent struts in a Supergirl costume — with toilet paper on her heel.
words.ety: Latin super (above) + cilium (eyelash) → supercilium, the eyebrow. Picture a snob raising an eyebrow.

words.d: loudly and offensively self-assertive; pushy
words.ex: A bumptious driver cut to the front of the traffic jam.
words.ety: Probably bump + presumptuous: someone who bumps you out of the way.

words.d: excessive pride or self-confidence that leads to downfall
words.ex: The CEO's hubris led him to ignore every warning.
words.ety: Greek: arrogance toward the gods. Odysseus taunted the blinded Cyclops with his real name — and Poseidon punished him for ten years. Adjective: hubristic.

words.d: pompous, inflated language with little substance
words.ex: The speech was all bombast and no plan.
words.ety: In the 1500s bombast was cotton stuffing for cushions — padding to fill something empty. Adjective: bombastic.

words.d: to talk at length in a pompous, boastful way
words.ex: The pundit bloviated for an hour without saying anything.
words.ety: An 1800s Americanism built on 'blow' — a blowhard full of hot air. Revived to describe President Harding's speeches.

words.d: a self-seeking flatterer who sucks up to people with power
words.ex: The sycophants who flattered the teacher all got A's.
words.ety: Vivid synonyms: bootlicker, toady, lickspittle, groveler.

words.d: excessively eager to please or obey; servile
words.ex: The obsequious butler agreed with every word his employer said.
words.ety: Latin sequ (follow), keyword sequence: obsequious people follow others around to gain favor.

words.d: to coax someone into or out of something with flattery and charm
words.ex: She wheedled her dad into lending her the car.
words.ety: Synonyms: cajole, coax. Typical pairs: wheedle into, wheedle out of.

words.d: flattering words or actions used to persuade
words.ex: He was deaf to the blandishments of his entourage.
words.ety: From Latin blandus (smooth, flattering).

words.d: excessively flattering and insincere in an oily, slick way
words.ex: The unctuous salesman oozed charm from every pore.
words.ety: Latin unctus (anointed with oil) — think oily. Down-to-earth synonym: smarmy.

words.d: full and resonant (of a voice); pompous and pretentious (of speech or writing)
words.ex: His orotund voice filled the hall.
words.ety: Latin ore rotundo, 'with a round mouth'. Positive for voices, negative for prose.

words.d: having knowledge of events before they happen; showing foresight
words.ex: A prescient economist predicted the crash years ahead.
words.ety: pre (before) + sci (know, as in science): knowing beforehand. Noun: prescience.

words.d: to release someone from slavery
words.ex: He manumitted the people he had enslaved in his will.
words.ety: Latin manus (hand) + mittere (send, let go): to release from one's hand. Noun: manumission; synonym: emancipate.

words.d: to outline sketchily; or to foreshadow vaguely
words.ex: The opening scene adumbrates the hero's fall.
words.ety: Latin umbra (shadow): to cast a faint shadow of what's to come.

words.d: offense or annoyance (usually 'take umbrage')
words.ex: She took umbrage at his remarks about her cooking.
words.ety: From umbra (shadow) → suspicion, the 'shady' feeling of being insulted.

words.d: unable to be avoided; inescapable
words.ex: Change is ineluctable.
words.ety: in (not) + eluctari (struggle out of).

words.d: too great or extreme to be expressed in words
words.ex: They felt ineffable joy at their daughter's birth.
words.ety: in (not) + effari (speak out).

words.d: a mild word substituted for one that seems too blunt or harsh
words.ex: 'Passed away' is a euphemism for 'died'.
words.ety: Greek eu (good) + pheme (speech).

words.d: pleasing to the ear
words.ex: She has a euphonious voice.
words.ety: Greek eu (good) + phon (sound).

words.d: arrogantly insisting that one's unproven opinions are true; closed-minded
words.ex: His dogmatic adherence to old methods bankrupted the firm.
words.ety: Greek dogma originally meant simply 'opinion, what one thinks is true'. Related: doctrinaire (rigidly sticking to a theory), imperious (overbearing).

words.d: to express opinions in a pompous, dogmatic way, usually at length
words.ex: My roommate pontificates about topics she knows nothing about.
words.ety: From pontiff (a high priest or pope). Picture a pompous preacher who never stops.

words.d: a person who abandons their religion, political party, principles or cause
words.ex: The group branded anyone who left as an apostate.
words.ety: Greek apo (away) + stenai (to stand): one who stands away from former beliefs. Noun: apostasy. (Apostle shares apo- but comes from 'send'.)

words.d: political propaganda spread through art, music, drama or literature
words.ex: The critic called the film left-wing agitprop — but entertaining.
words.ety: A portmanteau of agitation + propaganda, from a Soviet Communist Party department.

words.d: deceitful, treacherous and disloyal
words.ex: The perfidious soldier sold his general's plans to the enemy.
words.ety: Latin per (through, beyond) + fid (faith): going beyond the limits of trust. Noun: perfidy. Think Benedict Arnold.

words.d: open to more than one interpretation, often deliberately to mislead
words.ex: The suspect gave equivocal answers to direct questions.
words.ety: Latin equ (equal) + voc (voice, call): giving equal voice to different meanings. Verb: equivocate. Opposite: unequivocal.

words.d: unclear because it can be understood in more than one way
words.ex: 'Police discover crack in Australia' is an ambiguous headline.
words.ety: Latin ambi (both). Unlike equivocal, no intent to deceive is implied.

words.d: having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
words.ex: I'm ambivalent about moving — excited and anxious at once.
words.ety: Latin ambi (both) + valent (being strong): both sides pull equally.

words.d: to hide one's true feelings, motives or nature behind a false appearance
words.ex: He dissembled and told his aunt the meatloaf was delicious.
words.ety: Related to resemble (Latin simulare, to pretend): a dissembler tries to resemble something they're not.

words.d: shy and lacking self-confidence
words.ex: The diffident student rarely spoke up.
words.ety: dif (= dis, lack of) + fid (trust): lacking trust in oneself.

words.d: too ready to believe things; gullible
words.ex: Credulous investors fell for the scheme.
words.ety: Latin credere (believe). Opposite: incredulous (unwilling to believe, skeptical).

words.d: using very few words; terse
words.ex: My teenager's laconic answer to everything is 'good'.
words.ety: From Laconia, the region of Sparta. When Philip of Macedon threatened, 'If I enter Laconia, I will raze Sparta,' the Spartans replied with one word: 'If.' Opposite: loquacious.

words.d: brief but full of meaning and force
words.ex: The defense attorney's pithy argument won the case.
words.ety: From pith, the spongy core of a plant stem — the essential part. Related to pit (a peach pit). Think of Yoda's sayings.

words.d: strong public criticism or verbal abuse; the disgrace that results
words.ex: His unpopular vote brought obloquy from the opposition.
words.ety: Latin ob (against) + loq (speak): speech against someone.

words.d: to stir up or incite trouble, such as a riot or rebellion
words.ex: Agitators tried to foment an uprising.
words.ety: Hook: you stir up or whip up FOAM. Common pairs: foment a riot, foment rebellion.

words.d: to protest or denounce thunderously; also to explode violently
words.ex: The preacher fulminated against gambling and video games.
words.ety: Latin fulmen (lightning flash). Usually 'fulminate against'. Synonyms: rail against, upbraid, excoriate.

words.d: a bitter, violent verbal attack
words.ex: The losing coach launched into a fifteen-minute philippic against reporters.
words.ety: From Demosthenes' speeches denouncing King Philip of Macedon. Synonyms: invective, diatribe, tirade, harangue.

words.d: to speak or write about someone in an abusively disparaging way
words.ex: The scientist was vilified until other studies proved her right.
words.ety: Related to vile: you say vile things about someone. Cousins: malign, defame, denigrate, besmirch, sully.

words.d: a false statement made to damage someone's reputation; slander
words.ex: The neighbors' calumnies forced him to leave town.
words.ety: Stress on the first syllable: KAL-um-nee. Verb: calumniate.

words.d: to remove material considered offensive from a text, often prudishly
words.ex: The network bowdlerized the film for prime time.
words.ety: An eponym: Thomas Bowdler published 'The Family Shakespeare' (1818) with all the racy bits removed.

words.d: very talkative
words.ex: Our loquacious guide never paused for breath.
words.ety: Latin loq (speak). Opposite of laconic.

words.d: insulting, abusive language
words.ex: He hurled invective at the referee.
words.ety: Latin invehi (to attack). Related: vituperation (adj. vituperative).

words.d: to talk in a rambling, aimless or incoherent way
words.ex: He maundered on for twenty minutes without answering my question.
words.ety: Probably a variant of meander (to wander), from the winding Maeander River. The opposite of pithy. Synonyms: babble, prattle.

words.d: to expose someone to public ridicule and harsh criticism; (noun) a wooden frame that locked an offender's head and hands for public shaming
words.ex: The pitcher was pilloried by fans and press alike.
words.ety: Medieval pillories stood in marketplaces so passers-by could mock the guilty.

words.d: a long, bitter lament or list of complaints, often predicting doom
words.ex: Her column was another jeremiad about the decline of manners.
words.ety: Eponym: the prophet Jeremiah, who foretold and lamented the fall of Judah. Often 'a jeremiad against …'.

words.d: light, playful teasing banter
words.ex: Hepburn and Tracy were famous for their witty badinage.
words.ety: French badiner (to joke). Hook: two people 'bat' teasing remarks back and forth. Related: repartee, raillery; riposte = a quick, sharp comeback (from fencing).

words.d: a formal public speech or text of elaborate praise
words.ex: The general's panegyric for his fallen soldiers moved everyone.
words.ety: Greek pan (all) + agora (assembly): praise delivered to everyone gathered in the marketplace. Synonyms: encomium, tribute, homage.

words.d: an enthusiastic song or piece of writing praising something
words.ex: The film is a paean to working families.
words.ety: Originally a Greek hymn of thanks to Apollo. Pronounced PEE-un.

words.d: pretentious, insincere nonsense
words.ex: His fiery speech was mostly partisan claptrap.
words.ety: Literally a trick to trap an audience into clapping. Cousins: balderdash, poppycock, twaddle, codswallop, malarkey, hogwash, hooey.

words.d: nonsense; empty, untrue talk
words.ex: That miracle diet is pure bunk.
words.ety: Toponym: in 1820 Congressman Felix Walker gave an endless, empty speech 'for Buncombe', his county. Debunk = expose the nonsense.

words.d: idle chatter; also prolonged, tedious fuss or flattery
words.ex: The negotiator cut through the palaver to the real issues.
words.ety: From Portuguese palavra (word).

words.d: bland, simplistic or insipid ideas, speech or writing
words.ex: The report was intellectual pablum.
words.ety: Pablum was a mushy 1930s cereal for babies — soft, bland, easy to swallow. Synonym: pap.

words.d: a person in a conversation; often an informal go-between in negotiations
words.ex: A retired diplomat served as interlocutor between the two sides.
words.ety: Latin inter (between) + loc (speak).

words.d: a quick, clever reply to an insult or criticism
words.ex: Her witty riposte silenced the heckler.
words.ety: Fencing term for a quick counter-thrust after parrying.

words.d: excessively harsh and severe (of laws or punishments)
words.ex: The regime imposed draconian penalties on protesters.
words.ety: Draco, Athens' first lawgiver (c. 621 BCE), made almost every crime — even stealing a cabbage — punishable by death. Solon, his wiser successor, gave us 'solon' (a wise lawmaker).

words.d: idealistic, romantic and wildly impractical
words.ex: Their quixotic plan to beat the big-box stores was doomed.
words.ety: From Don Quixote, Cervantes' knight who tilted at windmills he mistook for giants.

words.d: to redraw voting districts to give one party an unfair advantage
words.ex: Critics accused the legislature of gerrymandering the map.
words.ety: Governor Elbridge Gerry's 1812 redistricting created a district shaped like a salamander: Gerry + salamander.

words.d: a traitor who collaborates with an occupying enemy
words.ex: The resistance despised the quislings who served the occupiers.
words.ety: Vidkun Quisling, the Norwegian who helped Nazi Germany occupy Norway in 1940 and was executed for treason in 1945.

words.d: a scene of uproar and wild confusion
words.ex: When the power failed, the stadium descended into bedlam.
words.ety: From the Hospital of St Mary of Bethlehem in London — 'Bedlam' — an asylum the public once visited for entertainment.

words.d: a person who opposes new technology
words.ex: I'm a Luddite when it comes to smart fridges.
words.ety: The Luddites (1811–16) were English workers who smashed new machinery, supposedly named after Ned Ludd. Hook: a Luddite is a fuddy-duddy about tech.

words.d: coarse, foul, abusive language
words.ex: The argument degenerated into billingsgate.
words.ety: A toponym: London's Billingsgate fish market, famous for its inventively profane fishmongers.

words.d: the mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, often comically
words.ex: 'He's a man of great statue' is a malapropism.
words.ety: Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's play The Rivals (1775), from French mal à propos (inappropriate).

words.d: a word derived from a person's name
words.ex: 'Sandwich' is an eponym of the Earl of Sandwich.
words.ety: Greek epi (upon) + onym (name). A toponym is a word derived from a place name.

words.d: appropriate, fitting; with reference to
words.ex: His remarks were apropos of the occasion.
words.ety: French à propos (to the purpose). Mal apropos = inappropriate.

words.d: reasoning from specific instances to a general principle
words.ex: By induction, she concluded that all the samples were contaminated.
words.ety: Bottom-up reasoning: in (into) + duc (lead).

words.d: reasoning from general premises to a specific, necessary conclusion
words.ex: All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal — that's deduction.
words.ety: de (down, from) + duc (lead): leading down from the general to the specific.

words.d: a critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture
words.ex: The professor's exegesis made the dense article finally make sense.
words.ety: Greek for 'explanation, interpretation'. Pronounced ek-suh-JEE-sis.

words.d: having keen insight and understanding; shrewd
words.ex: A perspicacious critic spotted the flaw everyone else missed.
words.ety: per (through) + spic (look): able to see through the surface — intellectual X-ray vision. Synonyms: astute, discerning, sagacious, sapient.

words.d: intended to teach, especially in a preachy or excessively moralizing way
words.ex: The film had a message but wasn't overly didactic.
words.ety: Greek didaskein (to teach). Related verb: sermonize.

words.d: overly concerned with minor details, rules or displaying learning
words.ex: Our pedantic guide corrected everyone's pronunciation.
words.hook: A mouse pad stuffs itself with tiny details until it's too big for the attic.
words.ety: From Greek ped (child) via pedagogue (teacher).

words.d: a person hostile or indifferent to culture, art and intellectual pursuits
words.ex: Only a philistine would call the museum a waste of space.
words.hook: A Philly cheesesteak shop so old people call it ancient — and it has no taste for art.
words.ety: The biblical Philistines; in 1687 university students in Jena used the German 'Philister' for anti-education townsfolk, and Matthew Arnold popularized it in English.

words.d: having or showing deep, extensive scholarly knowledge
words.ex: Her erudite lecture covered three centuries of history.
words.ety: Latin e (out of) + rudis (rough, untaught — as in rude): brought out of roughness by education. Noun: erudition.

words.d: little known and difficult to understand; profound
words.ex: The paper was too recondite to make an impact.
words.ety: Synonym: abstruse. Stresses depth and remoteness from everyday interests.

words.d: understood by only a small group with special knowledge
words.ex: Handyman skills remain esoteric to me.
words.ety: Greek esoterikos (belonging to an inner circle). Synonym: arcane.

words.d: showing dedication and diligence; persevering
words.ex: The carpenter's sedulous workmanship showed in every joint.
words.hook: Tiny seeds climb a steep hill with a shoelace, never giving up.
words.ety: Synonyms: diligent, assiduous, persistent, tenacious. Always hire a sedulous person.

words.d: done effortlessly and fluently; or (negatively) too easy, shallow and simplistic
words.ex: Her facile mind solved the puzzle at once. / His facile answers earned a D.
words.ety: Latin fac (do): doing things easily. Related: facility (aptitude), facilitate (make easier).

words.d: brisk, cheerful readiness and eagerness
words.ex: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.
words.ety: Synonyms: eagerness, zeal, vim and vigor, get-up-and-go.

words.d: habitually lazy; avoiding effort
words.ex: The indolent writer never got out of bed before noon.
words.ety: Say it slowly — it sounds lazy. Synonyms: slothful, lackadaisical, lethargic, listless, languid.

words.d: a state of physical or mental sluggishness and inactivity
words.ex: Free pizza roused the boys from their torpor.
words.ety: Latin torpere (to be numb). The torpedo was first a numbing electric fish. Adjective: torpid.

words.d: sluggish, lethargic and inactive
words.ex: The economy finally broke out of its torpid growth.
words.ety: Think of a teenager on a school morning.

words.d: cloudy and muddy with stirred-up sediment; also confused and muddled
words.ex: Rescuers couldn't see through the turbid floodwater.
words.ety: Latin turba (turmoil); keyword turbulent.

words.d: swollen; (of language) pompous and overblown
words.ex: The love song's turgid lyrics made us cringe.
words.ety: Hook: I URGe you not to write turgid prose. Hemingway is the opposite.

words.d: stubbornly or annoyingly persistent
words.ex: His pertinacious questioning exhausted the professor.
words.ety: Compare tenacious (admirably determined).

words.d: to stun or astonish; to make unable to think clearly
words.ex: The news stupefied the entire town.
words.ety: -fy (make) + stupor: to make into a stupor.

words.d: a split within a group into opposing factions
words.ex: The dispute caused a schism in the party.
words.ety: Greek schisma (cleft), related to scissors and schizophrenia. Pronounced SIZ-um or SKIZ-um. The Great Schism split the Christian church in 1054.

words.d: the scattering of a people away from their ancestral homeland; also the dispersed community itself
words.ex: The Irish diaspora spread across the world.
words.ety: Greek dia (across) + speirein (to scatter, sow). Capitalized for the Jewish Diaspora.

words.d: a gap or missing part, especially in a text or in knowledge
words.ex: A large lacuna at the start of the manuscript made it confusing.
words.ety: Latin lacuna (hole, pit), related to lake and lagoon — picture an empty lagoon. Plural: lacunae.

words.d: the jaws, mouth or throat of a hungry animal; figuratively, something that devours
words.ex: The tabloids feed the insatiable maw of public curiosity.
words.ety: Old English maga (stomach). Common phrase: the gaping maw of …

words.d: (1) to split or cut apart; (2) to cling or stick closely to
words.ex: A cleaver cleaves the meat. / He cleaved to his principles.
words.ety: A contronym — two different Germanic words that ended up spelled alike. The 'cling' sense is related to glue.

words.d: a series of linked things or events, like a chain
words.ex: A concatenation of small errors caused the meltdown.
words.ety: Latin con (together) + catena (chain).

words.d: a small secret group plotting together; or the plot itself
words.ex: A cabal of advisers plotted to seize control.
words.ety: From Kabbalah (Jewish mysticism); popularized by Charles II's ministers Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley and Lauderdale — whose initials spell C-A-B-A-L.

words.d: a small, close-knit group sharing an interest or purpose
words.ex: She belongs to a coterie of serious skiers.
words.ety: Related words: clique (exclusive), faction (dissenting), sect, circle, cadre.

words.d: a word that has two opposite meanings
words.ex: 'Sanction' is a contronym: it can mean approve or penalize.
words.ety: Also called a Janus word, after the two-faced Roman god of doorways (and January).

words.d: to strip bare; to deprive of something important
words.ex: Clear-cutting denuded the hillside of trees.
words.ety: de (away) + nudare (strip, make nude).

words.d: to formally give up a throne, power or responsibility
words.ex: Edward VIII abdicated in 1936 to marry Wallis Simpson.
words.ety: ab (away) + dic (speak): to 'speak away' one's office. Originally meant to disown one's children.

words.d: to deny or renounce; also to give up (responsibility, a right)
words.ex: He abnegated his former beliefs.
words.ety: ab (away) + negare (deny). Abdicate is reserved for high office; abnegate is more general. Noun: abnegation (self-denial).

words.d: the act of washing oneself, especially as a religious ritual
words.ex: He performed his morning ablutions before prayer.
words.ety: ab (away) + luere (wash): washing the dirt — or sin — away.

words.d: ridiculously old-fashioned; literally, from before the biblical Flood
words.ex: The firm's antediluvian attitude to the internet cost it a generation of customers.
words.ety: Latin ante (before) + diluvium (flood, deluge). Coined by Sir Thomas Browne in the 1600s.

words.d: to leave abruptly, often making off with something
words.ex: The other hiker absquatulated with our gear.
words.ety: A playful 1830s Americanism: ab (away) + squat — pop up from a squat and run. From the same fad as bloviate and discombobulate.

words.d: to confuse or disconcert
words.ex: The sudden change of plans discombobulated everyone.
words.ety: A whimsical 1830s American coinage — it sounds confusing.

words.d: the rejection of all religious and moral principles; belief that life is meaningless
words.ex: The novel's hero drifts into nihilism.
words.ety: Latin nihil (nothing) — as in a 'nil–nil' soccer score.

words.d: extreme self-absorption; (philosophy) the view that only one's own mind is sure to exist
words.ex: His solipsism made every conversation about himself.
words.ety: Latin solus (alone) + ipse (self). The solipsist's breakup line: 'It's not you, it's me.'

words.d: the view that whether God exists cannot be known
words.ex: His agnosticism set him apart from both believers and atheists.
words.ety: Coined by T. H. Huxley in 1869: Greek a (not) + gnosis (knowledge). Atheism = a (without) + theos (god): belief that there is no god.

words.d: able to change form or do many different things; versatile
words.ex: Meryl Streep is a protean actor.
words.ety: Proteus, the Greek sea god who could foretell the future and changed shape to avoid being caught.

words.d: bad-tempered, irritable and spiteful
words.ex: His blog is full of splenetic attacks on anyone who disagrees.
words.ety: From the spleen, which medieval medicine saw as the seat of bad temper. Hook: a splinter in your spleen would make anyone splenetic. Cousins: irascible, testy, dyspeptic, cantankerous.

words.d: unruly, rebellious and hard to manage; also quarrelsome
words.ex: The coach struggled with a fractious team. / They had a fractious relationship.
words.ety: Latin frangere (to break), keyword fracture: fractious people break rules and the peace. Close to contumacious and refractory.

words.d: harshness of tone or manner; also harsh, rough conditions
words.ex: The children heard the asperity in their father's voice and stopped.
words.ety: Latin asper (rough, harsh) — used for sour wine and hard times. Related: exasperate (to treat thoroughly harshly).

words.d: to pester someone with persistent, urgent requests
words.ex: My son importuned us for a fifth phone.
words.ety: Synonyms: badger, beseech, implore, hound, plead.

words.d: calm and unemotional by temperament (positive: composed; negative: apathetic)
words.ex: The phlegmatic firefighters stayed perfectly calm.
words.ety: Phlegm was one of the four bodily 'humors'; too much of it supposedly made you sluggish and apathetic. Picture Mr. Spock with a bad cold.

words.d: enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining
words.ex: The family was stoic in the face of adversity.
words.ety: From Stoicism, the philosophy Zeno taught at the Stoa (painted porch) in Athens around 300 BCE. Unlike phlegmatic, stoicism is self-discipline.

words.d: calm, dull and showing little emotion or interest; impassive
words.ex: The stolid clerk processed forms without looking up.
words.ety: Suggests heavy, plodding routine and unquestioning dullness.

words.d: to accustom someone to something unpleasant so they no longer feel it
words.ex: Years in the desert inured the hermit to cold and hunger.
words.ety: Usually 'inured to'. Related: ascetic (a person who practices severe self-denial).

words.d: easily angered; hot-tempered
words.ex: The irascible chef threw a pan across the kitchen.
words.ety: Latin ira (anger), as in ire.

words.d: fearless and adventurous, especially in enduring danger over time
words.ex: Intrepid explorers mapped the uncharted coast.
words.ety: in (not) + trepidus (alarmed, trembling) — not trembling. Related: trepidation. Synonym: undaunted.

words.d: courage and mental strength in enduring pain or adversity over the long haul
words.ex: Douglass showed remarkable fortitude in teaching himself to read.
words.ety: Latin fortis (strong), as in fort and fortify.

words.d: spirited courage and determination; nerve; also energy and know-how
words.ex: The rookie quarterback kept getting up — that kid's got moxie.
words.ety: From Moxie, an 1880s bitter soft drink advertised to 'build up your nerve'. Synonyms: grit, pluck, gumption, guts.

words.d: reckless boldness; rash disregard of consequences
words.ex: He had the temerity to answer his phone during the exam.
words.ety: Latin temere (rashly). Don't confuse with timorous (fearful).

words.d: shameless audacity; nerve that may shock others (admiring or disapproving)
words.ex: She had the chutzpah to tell the CEO he was running the company into the ground.
words.ety: Yiddish. Classic definition: a man who kills his parents, then begs the court for mercy because he's an orphan. Related: brazen, brash, cheeky, audacity.

words.d: a swaggering show of courage meant to impress, often hiding fear
words.ex: The young gunslinger's bravado couldn't hide his shaking hands.
words.ety: From Italian bravo — someone showing bravado wants a 'bravo!' Common phrase: false bravado.

words.d: empty, arrogant boasting; or a boastful person
words.ex: His tales of heroism were pure braggadocio.
words.ety: Braggadocchio, a boastful fake knight in Spenser's The Faerie Queene (1590).

words.d: showing nervousness or a lack of confidence; fearful
words.ex: The timorous third-grader trembled after facing the bully.
words.ety: Latin timere (to fear), like timid. Related: milquetoast (a timid person, from a 1920s comic strip), milksop.

words.d: contemptibly cowardly
words.ex: The captain's craven refusal to fight led to mutiny.
words.ety: Hook: the raven made Poe's narrator craven.

words.d: lacking courage or determination; faint-hearted
words.ex: It was pusillanimous of him to stay silent while his friend was blamed.
words.ety: Latin pusillus (very small) + animus (spirit): small-spirited. Opposite: magnanimous (great-spirited, generous).

words.d: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
words.ex: She was magnanimous in victory.
words.ety: Latin magn (great) + animus (spirit).

words.d: carefree and unconcerned; nonchalant
words.ex: He took an insouciant stroll through town with his espresso.
words.ety: French in (not) + soucier (to worry). Hook: insouciant → loosey-goosey. Synonyms: breezy, debonair, jaunty.

words.d: very difficult to understand; obscure
words.ex: Finnegans Wake is famously abstruse.
words.ety: Latin abstrusus (concealed). A notch beyond recondite.

words.d: a sudden, striking realization or insight
words.ex: Each story in Dubliners turns on a character's epiphany.
words.ety: Greek epiphaneia (manifestation). Joyce popularized the literary sense.

words.d: vigorous, clear and incisive; sometimes cutting
words.ex: Uncle Jim's trenchant analysis went straight to the heart of the issue.
words.ety: Old French trenchant (cutting), related to trench — originally a cut in wood or earth.

words.d: having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or hidden way
words.ex: He warned us about the pernicious effects of smoking.
words.ety: Latin pernicies (ruin, destruction).

words.d: done secretly because it would not be approved of
words.ex: She sneaked a surreptitious glance at her phone.
words.ety: Latin surripere (to seize secretly).

words.d: the killing of a parent or close relative; or the person who does it
words.ex: Lizzie Borden was tried for parricide and acquitted.
words.ety: Hook: par- → parents + cide (kill). Related: matricide, patricide, fratricide (brother), sororicide (sister), regicide (king).

words.d: a pause or break in a line of verse or music, or in speech
words.ex: 'Once upon a midnight dreary, ‖ while I pondered' has a caesura.
words.ety: Latin caedere (to cut) — a cut in the line. Plural: caesurae.

words.d: surgery on a living animal for research; figuratively, a ruthless, detailed critique
words.ex: The press's vivisection of the general forced his resignation.
words.ety: Latin vivus (alive) + sect (cut).

words.d: a state of disuse or inactivity
words.ex: The old law has fallen into desuetude.
words.ety: Latin de (away from) + suescere (become accustomed). Usually 'fall into desuetude'. Pronounced DES-wi-tood.

words.d: eternal damnation; or utter ruin
words.ex: The preacher warned that sinners were on the road to perdition.
words.ety: Latin perdere (to destroy, lose).

words.d: to root out and destroy completely
words.ex: Black bears were extirpated from the region by 2003.
words.ety: Latin ex (out) + stirps (root, stem): to pull out by the roots. Synonyms: eradicate, exterminate, uproot.

words.d: to formally repeal or abolish (a law, treaty); or to neglect a duty
words.ex: Critics say Congress abrogated its duty to declare war.
words.ety: Latin abrogare (to repeal).

words.d: the end of a century, especially the late 1800s and its sophisticated, decadent mood
words.ex: Fin-de-siècle Vienna was a hub for artists.
words.ety: French 'end of the century'. English equivalent: turn of the century.

words.d: clear, sharp and penetrating (of thought or remarks)
words.ex: She offered an incisive analysis of the problem.
words.ety: From cise (cut): remarks that cut to the heart of the matter.

words.d: to strike hard; to defeat or kill (past: smote)
words.ex: Cain smote his brother Abel.
words.ety: Related to smitten — struck hard by love.

words.d: a choice between taking what is offered or nothing at all; (loosely) a choice between two bad options
words.ex: It was a Hobson's choice: the full sports package or no soccer channel.
words.ety: Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge stable keeper (c. 1600), let customers take the horse nearest the door — or none — so his horses were rested equally.

words.d: to make someone dull, bored or ineffective; to stifle
words.ex: The rigid rules stultified creativity in the office.
words.ety: Word-part hook: stul → dull. Adjective: stultifying.

words.d: a sudden thrilling shiver of excitement or fear
words.ex: A frisson of fear ran through me as I climbed to the attic.
words.ety: French 'shiver', from Latin frigere (to be cold) — like frigid. Pronounced free-SOHN.

words.d: debris; waste or leftover fragments
words.ex: The detritus of the battle littered the streets.
words.ety: Latin deterere (to wear away), like detriment: detritus is what's left after things wear away.

words.d: a word, phrase or custom that distinguishes members of a group; also an old slogan still clung to
words.ex: Saying 'Derry' or 'Londonderry' can act as a shibboleth in Northern Ireland.
words.ety: In the Book of Judges, fleeing Ephraimites were caught because they couldn't pronounce the 'sh' in shibboleth.

words.d: the specialized vocabulary of a particular group (originally thieves)
words.ex: Hikers have their own argot: NOBOs, SOBOs and slackpacking.
words.ety: French, 1860; originally the slang of Paris rogues. Pronounced AR-go or AR-gut. Not related to the Argonauts.

words.d: a regional or social variety of a language, with its own words, pronunciation and grammar
words.ex: In Pittsburgh's dialect, soda is 'pop'.
words.ety: Greek dialektos (way of speaking).

words.d: the everyday language spoken by ordinary people, as opposed to formal or literary language
words.ex: Luther translated the Bible into the German vernacular.
words.ety: Hook: Vern is a regular guy who uses everyday words.

words.d: technical or specialized language that is hard for outsiders to understand
words.ex: To me, ballet terminology is pure jargon.
words.ety: Old French jargoun (twittering of birds).

words.d: a common language used between speakers of different native languages
words.ex: English has become a global lingua franca for business.
words.ety: Italian 'Frankish tongue': a mixed trade language of Renaissance Mediterranean ports. Also called a bridge language.

words.d: rambling from topic to topic; digressive
words.ex: The comedian's discursive stories somehow worked.
words.ety: Latin discurrere (to run to and fro). Hook: like a meandering current.

words.d: a nickname, often humorous or affectionate
words.ex: 'The Big Easy' is a sobriquet for New Orleans.
words.ety: Old French for 'a chuck under the chin'. Pronounced SOH-bri-kay.

words.d: given to using long words; (of words) very long
words.ex: The student hid his confusion behind sesquipedalian words.
words.ety: From Horace's 'sesquipedalia verba' — words a foot and a half long: sesqui (one and a half) + ped (foot).

words.d: talking in one's sleep
words.ex: His somniloquy kept his roommate awake.
words.ety: Latin somnus (sleep, as in insomnia) + loq (speak).

words.d: an accidental swap of the first sounds of two words, often with funny results
words.ex: 'A well-boiled icicle' for 'a well-oiled bicycle' is a spoonerism.
words.ety: Rev. William Archibald Spooner of Oxford, famous for slips like 'The Lord is a shoving leopard'.

words.d: a word that sounds the same as another but has a different spelling and meaning
words.ex: 'Patience' and 'patients' are homophones.
words.ety: Greek homo (same) + phon (sound).

words.d: a word spelled like another but with a different pronunciation and meaning
words.ex: 'Minute' (60 seconds) and 'minute' (tiny) are homographs.
words.ety: Greek homo (same) + graph (write).

words.d: a word spelled and pronounced like another but with a different meaning
words.ex: 'Bear' the animal and 'bear' a burden are homonyms.
words.ety: Greek homo (same) + onym (name). Also called multiple-meaning words; contronyms (cleave, sanction, dust) are a special kind.

words.d: a word derived from a place name
words.ex: Tuxedo, hamburger and Bordeaux are toponyms.
words.ety: Greek topos (place) + onym (name). Tuxedo Park, New York, gave us the tailless dinner jacket.

words.d: a word formed from the first letters of a phrase
words.ex: Scuba stands for 'self-contained underwater breathing apparatus'.
words.ety: Greek akros (tip) + onym: a word made from the tips of other words. Letter-by-letter ones (FBI) are sometimes called initialisms.

words.d: a word blending the sounds and meanings of two others
words.ex: Brunch, motel, smog and chortle are portmanteau words.
words.ety: Coined by Lewis Carroll (Humpty Dumpty: 'two meanings packed up into one word'). A portmanteau is a two-compartment suitcase.

words.d: a word shortened without changing its meaning
words.ex: 'Gym' is clipped from 'gymnasium'.
words.ety: Canter is clipped from 'Canterbury trot', the pace of pilgrims riding to Becket's shrine.

words.d: to refuse to buy, use or deal with something as a protest
words.ex: Customers boycotted the store.
words.ety: An eponym: Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent shunned by the whole community in 1880 for refusing to lower rents.

words.d: prudish insistence on conventional propriety
words.ex: The censors' Grundyism banned the play.
words.ety: Mrs. Grundy, an unseen prude in Thomas Morton's 1798 play Speed the Plough: 'What would Mrs. Grundy say?'

words.d: a chaotic situation, especially a recurring muddle
words.ex: Another booking snafu left us without a room.
words.ety: A WWII military acronym: 'situation normal, all fouled up' (politely).

words.d: extremely infectious or harmful (of a disease); bitterly hostile (of words or feelings)
words.ex: The Black Death was a virulent plague. / He launched a virulent personal attack.
words.ety: Latin virus (poison). Synonyms for the figurative sense: acerbic, caustic, acrimonious, vitriolic.

words.d: bitingly sarcastic, often with ill intent
words.ex: Her mordant remarks made colleagues avoid her.
words.hook: The more coffee the ants drink, the more biting their sarcastic jokes get.
words.ety: Latin mordere (to bite), like morsel and remorse (the past coming back to bite you). Compare caustic, acrid, scathing (fierce but often righteous).

words.d: pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste; also stimulating, provocative or charming
words.ex: My son loved the piquant taste of lemons. / We had a piquant debate.
words.ety: French piquer (to prick, sting). Related: pique (to irritate; or to arouse curiosity: 'it piqued my interest'). Opposite: insipid.

words.d: aggressively eager to offer unwanted help or advice; meddlesome
words.ex: The officious waiter practically ordered our meal for us.
words.ety: Latin officium (duty, service), like office. In the 1560s it meant 'eager to serve'; by 1600 'too eager'.

words.d: good for one's health; wholesome
words.ex: The salubrious sea air made me feel healthier.
words.ety: Latin salus (health). Opposite: insalubrious.

words.d: producing a beneficial effect, especially an improvement or useful lesson
words.ex: Unstructured play has a salutary effect on children's development.
words.ety: Same root as salute and salutation — Romans greeted each other with 'Salve!' (be well).

words.d: kind, friendly and indulgent, like an uncle
words.ex: The avuncular judge gave the young man a second chance.
words.ety: Latin avunculus (maternal uncle), the source of 'uncle'.

words.d: having masculine strength and energy
words.ex: The ad featured a virile lumberjack.
words.ety: Latin vir (man) — not related to virulent.

words.d: very small in amount; meager and inadequate
words.ex: The boy tried to stretch his exiguous lunch.
words.ety: Related to exact: exiguous = less than the exact amount you need. Common pair: exiguous resources.

words.d: a gradual decrease in loudness or intensity
words.ex: The chorus ended in a haunting diminuendo.
words.ety: Italian, related to diminish. Opposite: crescendo.

words.d: very small; also trivial or petty
words.ex: Our worries about dinner seem Lilliputian next to theirs.
words.ety: Lilliput, the land of tiny, petty people in Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), who fought over which end to crack an egg.

words.d: gigantic; enormous
words.ex: Brobdingnagian sculptures towered over the entrance.
words.ety: Brobdingnag, the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels. A big, clunky word for big things. Informal cousin: ginormous (gigantic + enormous).

words.d: an artist's or writer's greatest work
words.ex: Fallingwater is often called Frank Lloyd Wright's magnum opus.
words.ety: Latin 'great work'. Plural: magna opera. Synonyms: masterpiece, chef-d'oeuvre.

words.d: comfortably and conveniently roomy
words.ex: The dorm room was surprisingly commodious.
words.ety: Latin commodus (convenient) — the same source as commode, a convenient chamber-pot chair.

words.d: able to hold a great deal; roomy
words.ex: Aunt Thelma has a capacious memory.
words.ety: Related to capable and capacity: capacious = capable of holding a lot (and it rhymes with spacious).

words.d: a huge, overwhelming force that crushes everything in its path
words.ex: At 16, Tommy was a juggernaut on the football field.
words.ety: From Jagannath ('lord of the world'), a form of Krishna, whose giant festival chariots are pulled through Puri, India. Anglicized by the 'Hobson-Jobson' process.

words.d: extremely small
words.ex: The diminutive dancer commanded the stage.
words.ety: Latin min (small).

words.d: a person obsessed with their own power and importance
words.ex: The villain was a classic megalomaniac.
words.ety: Greek mega (great) + mania (madness).

words.d: the smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning in a language
words.ex: 'Bat' and 'pat' differ by a single phoneme.
words.hook: Pho and foe sound the same when you slurp noodles sitting on your knees.

words.d: a strong desire to travel and explore the world
words.ex: Her wanderlust took her to forty countries before thirty.
words.ety: Borrowed from German wandern (to hike) + Lust (desire).

words.d: the logical but non-standard spellings young children create (like YIZ for 'wise')
words.ex: Invented spelling shows what a child knows about sounds.
words.ety: Children who spell by letter names use Y for the 'w' sound because the name 'why' starts with it.

words.d: to submit obsequiously; to yield weakly to someone more powerful
words.ex: My brother refused to truckle to the bullies.
words.ety: A truckle (trundle) bed was the low bed servants slept on, beneath their master's. Usually 'truckle to'.

words.d: promoting a particular, often controversial, point of view; biased
words.ex: His tendentious argument ignored all the research.
words.ety: Related to tendency (leaning) and tenet (a belief one holds): leaning so far one way you can't see the others.

words.d: a ringing or tinkling sound, especially of bells
words.ex: The tintinnabulation of church bells filled the valley.
words.ety: Latin tintinnabulum (bell); compare tinnitus (ringing in the ears). Poe used it in 'The Bells'.

words.d: a soft whispering or rustling sound; a murmur
words.ex: The susurration of the waves lulled us to sleep.
words.ety: Latin susurrus (whisper) — say it and you hear it.

words.d: to clear one's throat pompously, especially to show disapproval; to grumble
words.ex: The professor harrumphed before answering.
words.ety: An imitation of the sound itself.

words.d: a word that habitually appears alongside another
words.ex: 'Against' is a collocate of 'fulminate'.
words.ety: Latin com (together) + locare (to place): words placed together.

words.d: pleasure taken in someone else's misfortune
words.ex: I felt a twinge of schadenfreude when our rivals lost too.
words.ety: German Schaden (harm) + Freude (joy).

words.d: the defining spirit or mood of a particular period
words.ex: Jazz and flappers captured the zeitgeist of the 1920s.
words.hook: A guy sightseeing with binoculars sees his grandpa's college days — a whole generation's mood.
words.ety: German Zeit (time) + Geist (spirit, ghost).

words.d: sadness and weariness at the evils and suffering of the world
words.ex: Reading the news filled her with weltschmerz.
words.ety: German Welt (world) + Schmerz (pain).

words.d: a powerful adviser who works behind the scenes; (later, loosely) a respected elder statesman
words.ex: Many saw the chief of staff as the éminence grise of the administration.
words.ety: French 'grey eminence': Father Joseph, the grey-robed Capuchin adviser to Cardinal Richelieu (the 'red eminence').

words.d: a person who stays neutral or can't make up their mind, especially in politics
words.ex: The senator was too much of a mugwump to take a stand.
words.ety: From an Algonquian word for 'important person'; in 1884 it mocked Republicans who left their party. A fun false story: a bird with its mug on one side of the fence and its wump on the other.

words.d: a person or thing especially disliked or dreaded
words.ex: The Joker is Batman's bête noire.
words.ety: French 'black beast'. Synonyms: nemesis, bugbear, anathema.

words.d: a ghostly double of a living person; (now often) someone who looks strikingly like another
words.ex: I saw your doppelgänger at the grocery store.
words.ety: German 'double-goer'. Poe's story 'William Wilson' is a classic doppelgänger tale.

words.d: a word adopted from another language
words.ex: 'Kindergarten' is a German loanword.
words.ety: Linguists call the process lexical borrowing.

words.d: an embarrassing social blunder
words.ex: Asking about 'Londonderry' was a faux pas.
words.ety: French 'false step'.

words.d: the exact, most appropriate word or expression
words.ex: She searched for the mot juste to end her speech.
words.ety: French 'the exact word'. Hook: the JUST-right word.

words.d: a witty remark; a clever saying
words.ex: He was famous for his bons mots at dinner parties.
words.ety: French 'good word'.

words.d: an organized whole that is more than the sum of its parts
words.ex: Listeners grasp a story's gestalt rather than counting its words.
words.ety: German 'shape, form'. Gestalt psychology: we perceive wholes first (think of the face/vase illusion).

words.d: prestige or distinction; a mark of status
words.ex: Wearing that brand carried a certain cachet on campus.
words.ety: French 'seal' on a letter → a distinguishing mark → prestige. Pronounced ka-SHAY.

words.d: a hidden store of goods, valuables or weapons; the hiding place itself
words.ex: Soldiers found a cache of weapons in the cave.
words.ety: French cacher (to hide). Pronounced CASH — think stash.

words.d: a secret agent who incites others to break the law so they can be punished
words.ex: The lawsuit claimed the police used an agent provocateur.
words.ety: French; related to provoke — the agent's job is to provoke.

words.d: composure and calm under pressure
words.ex: Joe Montana's sangfroid won four Super Bowls.
words.ety: French sang (blood) + froid (cold): cool-bloodedness. Froid comes from Latin frigidus — like frigid, frozen. Synonym: aplomb.

words.d: self-confidence and poise, especially in a demanding situation
words.ex: She handled the hecklers with aplomb.
words.ety: French à plomb (upright, by the plumb line).

words.d: a small extra gift given with a purchase; a bonus
words.ex: The barista threw in a scone as lagniappe.
words.ety: New Orleans Creole from Spanish la ñapa (the gift). Mark Twain called it 'a word worth traveling to New Orleans to get'. Pronounced LAN-yap.

words.d: warm, cozy friendliness and comfort, with a sense of belonging
words.ex: Our Thanksgiving table is full of gemütlichkeit.
words.ety: German Gemüt (soul, feeling), cognate with English mood.

words.d: the ideas and feelings a word suggests beyond its literal meaning
words.ex: 'Request' has a more formal connotation than 'ask'.
words.ety: Its partner term is denotation, the literal dictionary meaning.

words.d: a decisive, finishing blow or remark; also something exceptional
words.ex: Her closing argument was a real sockdolager.
words.ety: An 1830s Americanism, perhaps a joke on 'doxology' (the hymn at the end of a service). A form of it ('sockdologizing') was the punchline Booth waited for before shooting Lincoln. Hook: you SOCK someone and they don't get up.

words.d: slightly hungry; also irritable
words.ex: A long hike always makes me peckish.
words.ety: Literally 'inclined to peck' — like a bird nibbling. Hobbits avoid it with second breakfast and elevenses.

words.d: quickly fading or disappearing; fleeting
words.ex: Rainbows are beautiful but evanescent.
words.ety: Latin e (= ex, out) + vanescere (to vanish). Hook: the VAN in evanescent → vanish.

words.d: weak and ineffective; or lazy and irresponsible
words.ex: The feckless leader was a mere figurehead.
words.ety: Scottish feck (a clipped form of effect) + -less: without effect.

words.d: a recklessly extravagant, self-indulgent person; wildly wasteful or dissolute
words.ex: The profligate rock star blew his millions on yachts.
words.ety: Latin profligare (to ruin, overthrow).

words.d: a newly coined word or expression
words.ex: 'Selfie' was once a neologism.
words.ety: Greek neo (new) + logos (word). A nonce word is invented for a single occasion.

words.d: an idea, behavior or style that spreads by imitation; especially an image or phrase that goes viral online
words.ex: The 'most interesting man in the world' became a meme.
words.ety: Coined by Richard Dawkins (1976) from Greek mimeme (imitated thing), shortened to rhyme with 'gene'. Related to mime and mimic.

words.d: an elementary particle that makes up protons and neutrons
words.ex: Protons are made of three quarks.
words.ety: Physicist Murray Gell-Mann took the spelling from Joyce's Finnegans Wake ('Three quarks for Muster Mark!') — fitting, since quarks come in threes.

words.d: a person who lacks a particular skill or knowledge; (in Harry Potter) a non-magical person
words.ex: Among my astrophysicist friends, I'm a complete muggle.
words.ety: Coined by J. K. Rowling from British slang 'mug' (a gullible person). Now in the Oxford English Dictionary.

words.d: well-meaning and kindly
words.ex: A benevolent neighbor shoveled our driveway without being asked.
words.hook: Your dog has been kind all week, so you give him a bone tucked inside an envelope.

words.d: showy but cheap and of poor quality
words.ex: The shop was full of tawdry souvenirs that broke within a day.
words.hook: A cheap, flashy towel that can't dry anything — it's tawdry.
words.ety: From 'tawdry lace', a corruption of St. Audrey's lace — cheap lace sold at St. Audrey's fair in England.

words.d: weak or slow; relaxed and lacking energy
words.ex: We spent a languid afternoon dozing by the pool.
words.hook: A squid lies limp in the middle of a bowling lane, too weak and lazy to move.

words.d: fond of company; sociable
words.ex: Her gregarious brother knew everyone at the party within an hour.
words.hook: A gray car packed with grains of rice, all chatting and partying together.

words.d: physical beauty
words.ex: Poets have praised the pulchritude of the valley for centuries.
words.hook: A toad at the poker table draws a straight flush — and a beautiful princess appears.
words.ety: Latin pulcher, beautiful.

words.d: loud, confused noise or disorder, especially from a crowd
words.ex: The announcement was lost in the tumult of the cheering fans.
words.hook: A giant tooth mows the lawn at dawn and the whole street erupts in angry shouting.

words.d: the act of reading or examining something, often carefully
words.ex: After a quick perusal of the menu, we ordered the soup.
words.hook: A parrot sprinkles salt on the book he's carefully reading.

words.d: strongly fragrant; also, strongly suggestive of something
words.ex: The kitchen was redolent of cinnamon and fresh bread.
words.hook: You swipe on a red deodorant and suddenly you smell sweet and fragrant.

words.d: a loud, hearty laugh; to laugh loudly
words.ex: His guffaw echoed across the quiet library.
words.hook: A clown juggles golf balls, they all bonk him on the head, and he lets out a huge laugh.

words.d: humiliation or degradation; being brought low
words.ex: He refused the job because he saw it as an abasement of his talents.
words.hook: Someone gets shoved down into the basement in front of everyone — total humiliation.

words.d: a person who publicly supports a cause; to publicly recommend or support
words.ex: She advocated for better pay for teachers.
words.hook: An avocado grabs the microphone to praise the carrot who's running for Congress.
words.ety: Latin ad (to) + vocare (to call). The same root: vocation (a calling), avocation (a hobby), convoke (call together), evoke (call forth), vocal.

words.d: to calm someone's anger; to win over or make peace
words.ex: He tried to conciliate his angry neighbor with a fresh pie.
words.hook: A kid hands his furious mom a latte-flavored ice-cream cone to calm her down.

words.d: drawing from a wide, diverse range of sources or styles
words.ex: His music taste is eclectic: jazz, punk and Malian blues.
words.hook: A man on an electric guitar switches between every genre imaginable.

words.d: to officially clear someone of blame
words.ex: New DNA evidence exonerated the prisoner after ten years.
words.hook: The rat ate the egg salad, not the monkey — so the monkey is set free from prison.
words.ety: Latin ex (out) + onus (burden): to lift the burden of guilt.

words.d: silly; lacking sense or meaning
words.ex: The comments section was full of inane arguments.
words.hook: In-N-Out is out of hamburgers? That makes no sense.

words.d: the ability to make good judgments and quick decisions
words.ex: Her business acumen turned a tiny stall into a chain of shops.
words.hook: Men sprint along an acute angle straight toward a giant brain.

words.d: relating to or befitting a son or daughter
words.ex: He visited his parents every Sunday out of filial devotion.
words.hook: A father takes his daughter to get her nails filed — an act of family affection.

words.d: to praise highly
words.ex: Critics lauded the film as a masterpiece.
words.hook: A church full of people raising their voices to praise the Lord.

words.d: casually calm and unconcerned
words.ex: He gave a nonchalant shrug when he heard he'd won.
words.hook: A nun faces the big Bible challenge totally calm — she's prepared for months.

words.d: a special benefit or privilege that comes with a position (a 'perk')
words.ex: A company car was one of the perquisites of the job.
words.hook: The pear is the star of the cuisine because it comes with so many health perks.
words.ety: Latin, an acquisition. The short form perk dates from the 1820s.

words.d: something out of its proper time period
words.ex: A wristwatch in a film about ancient Rome is an anachronism.
words.hook: Ants run wild inside a chrome watch, throwing time completely out of order.

words.d: an alliance, often temporary, of groups or parties
words.ex: Three parties formed a coalition to govern.
words.hook: Lumps of coal team up and burn together brightly — but only for a short while.

words.d: a scarcity or lack of something
words.ex: There is a dearth of affordable housing in the city.
words.hook: The Earth goes dark because there's a total lack of sunlight.

words.d: to publicly approve or support
words.ex: The union endorsed her campaign for mayor.
words.hook: A carpenter signs and stamps every door he builds — his seal of approval.

words.d: done without good reason; also, given free of charge
words.ex: The movie was spoiled by gratuitous violence.
words.hook: King Tut gets stuffed into a crate for absolutely no reason.

words.d: marrying someone while still married to another person
