words.ex: He was charged with bigamy when his first wife appeared.
words.hook: A big army officer has one wife in France and another in Germany.

words.d: fond of joking; playful and humorous
words.ex: His jocular tone put the nervous students at ease.
words.hook: A muscular jock keeps cracking jokes about being the strongest kid in school.

words.d: a person who owns and rents out land, buildings or apartments
words.ex: Our landlord finally fixed the heating.
words.hook: A farmer owns acres of land full of pigs — future lard.

words.d: a long triangular flag, especially one marking a championship
words.ex: The team hung its championship pennant in the gym.
words.hook: Winners at summer camp write their team name on a flag with a pen and hang it on their tent.

words.d: to cause severe destruction to
words.ex: The storm ravaged the coastal villages.
words.hook: A tornado hits a sewage-covered roof and tears it to pieces.

words.d: known or understood by only a few; mysterious
words.ex: The tax code is full of arcane rules.
words.hook: Only one kid in the whole arcade knows the secret to beating the game.

words.d: a division into two sharply contrasting parts
words.ex: There's often a dichotomy between what people say and what they do.
words.hook: A flower dies and the economy doesn't care — two completely separate things.

words.d: to judge in advance, without enough evidence
words.ex: Don't forejudge the new coach before her first game.
words.hook: A judge slams the gavel on a prisoner with a forehead tattoo — before hearing any evidence.

words.d: to seize power or a position without the right to it
words.ex: The general tried to usurp the throne.
words.hook: A waiter grabs your friend's surfboard without permission and won't give it back.

words.d: a soft, gentle breeze
words.ex: A cool zephyr drifted in from the sea.
words.hook: Zephyrus, the Greek god of the gentle west wind, blows a cool breeze.

words.d: disappointed on discovering something is not as good as believed
words.ex: Many voters grew disillusioned with the party.
words.hook: A disc promises amazing music, but it's an illusion — the crowd feels let down and ill.

words.d: gushing; expressing feelings in an unrestrained way
words.ex: She was effusive in her thanks.
words.hook: A tiny fuse bursts with so much energy it gushes sparks everywhere.
words.ety: Latin effundere, to pour out.

words.d: the point on which a lever pivots; a central supporting element
words.ex: Trust is the fulcrum of any partnership.
words.hook: A falcon balances on the very top of a car rim, pivoting there.

words.d: rudely disrespectful (noun: insolence)
words.ex: The insolent reply earned him detention.
words.hook: The sun crashes the party, dances wildly and burns everyone — so rude.

words.d: a comparison showing similarity between things otherwise unlike
words.ex: She used the analogy of a river to explain blood flow.
words.hook: Ants compare the ridges on a log to the veins of a leaf.

words.d: relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside
words.ex: They moved to a bucolic village with one shop and many sheep.
words.hook: A farmer watches his broccoli grow through binoculars from his farmhouse.
words.ety: Greek boukolos, herdsman (bous, ox).

words.d: moral correctness; honesty and integrity
words.ex: The judge was known for her rectitude.
words.hook: Two geologists judge rocks correctly and honestly — and keep great attitudes.

words.d: lending money at unreasonably high interest
words.ex: The law protects borrowers from usury.
words.hook: Sally selling seashells by the seashore gets charged rent at a crazy interest rate.

words.d: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
words.ex: The capricious weather ruined our picnic plans.
words.hook: Sometimes the Capri Sun pouch is full, sometimes empty — you never know.

words.d: an invented lie; also, the act of making something
words.ex: His story about the robbery was a complete fabrication.
words.hook: A mother stitches fabric together into something new — invented from scratch.

words.d: to write, carve or engrave words on a surface
words.ex: They inscribed her name on the trophy.
words.hook: An insect tries to write in the wind but can only scribble.

words.d: a painful or difficult experience that tests endurance
words.ex: Crossing the desert on foot was an ordeal.
words.hook: Kayakers use their oars to deal with a brutal, fast river current.

words.d: to outweigh; to be greater in number, weight or importance
words.ex: In the end, the arguments for staying preponderated.
words.hook: A deer gobbles meal prep and gets so heavy it almost sinks in the pond.

words.d: the ability to keep going despite hardship or fatigue
words.ex: Marathons test endurance more than speed.
words.hook: Dip Dorito after Dorito — the ranch just never runs out.

words.d: to gradually put an idea or feeling into someone's mind
words.ex: Good coaches instill confidence in their players.
words.hook: The dentist slowly puts a steel implant into a patient's mouth.

words.d: active or happening at night
words.ex: Owls are nocturnal hunters.
words.hook: Late at night a driver turns the wrong way and knocks down a stop sign.

words.d: the quality of being especially noticeable or important
words.ex: The salience of the issue grew after the flood.

words.d: understood or implied without being said
words.ex: Their silence gave tacit approval to the plan.
words.ety: Latin tacere, to be silent — also the root of taciturn (reserved, saying little).

words.d: a claim or accusation made without proof yet
words.ex: The company denied the allegations of fraud.

words.d: easily fooled or cheated
words.ex: Gullible investors lost their savings to the scheme.

words.d: kindly and gentle; favorable; (medicine) not harmful
words.ex: The tumor turned out to be benign.

words.d: on the outer edge; hence, minor or not essential
words.ex: Let's skip the peripheral issues and focus on cost.

words.d: to reject bluntly; a blunt refusal
words.ex: She rebuffed his offer of help.

words.d: strong dislike or ill will
words.ex: There was long-standing animosity between the rivals.

words.d: thin, slight, flimsy; weakly supported
words.ex: The link between the two cases is tenuous at best.

words.d: smugly self-satisfied and unaware of dangers or others' needs
words.ex: Winning three years in a row made the team complacent.

words.d: the highest point; the peak of achievement
words.ex: At the acme of her career she ran three companies.
words.ety: Straight from Greek akme, highest point. Elster remembers it through Wile E. Coyote's Acme products — and the cliffs he falls off.

words.d: no longer existing, operating or in use
words.ex: The factory has been defunct for a decade.
words.ety: Latin defunctus, dead, finished.

words.d: to encourage or assist, often in wrongdoing
words.ex: He was charged with aiding and abetting the robbery.

words.d: looking exhausted, worn out and gaunt
words.ex: After three sleepless nights she looked haggard.

words.d: to give up a right or claim voluntarily; to set aside
words.ex: He waived his right to a jury trial.

words.d: relating to the body's physical, especially sexual, appetites
words.ex: The sermon warned against carnal desires.

words.d: to give official approval to; official permission (also, as a noun, a penalty)
words.ex: The board sanctioned the merger.

words.d: a person who wastes money; wasteful
words.ex: His spendthrift habits drove the company into debt.

words.d: to calm or soothe someone's anger; to soften
words.ex: Nothing the manager said could mollify the angry customer.
words.ety: Latin mollis (soft) + facere (to make): to make soft. Cousin: emollient, a softening cream.

words.d: perfectly clear; having only one possible meaning
words.ex: The answer was an unequivocal no.

words.d: able to be shaped or molded; easily influenced
words.ex: Young minds are malleable.
words.ety: Latin malleus, hammer: capable of being hammered into shape. Compare tractable (from tractare, to handle — as in tractor).

words.d: using more words than needed; wordy
words.ex: The verbose memo could have been a single paragraph.
words.ety: Latin verbum, word — also verbal, verbatim (word for word) and verbiage (excess words).

words.d: lasting only a short time; a person passing through
words.ex: The town's transient population swells every summer.

words.d: to reject firmly; to refuse to accept or be associated with
words.ex: The senator repudiated the extremist group's endorsement.

words.d: acting quickly without thinking; impulsively eager
words.ex: In an impetuous moment he quit his job.

words.d: careful and sparing with money; inexpensive
words.ex: They ate a frugal meal of soup and bread.
words.ety: Latin frux, fruit: careful with the fruit of one's labor.

words.d: out of place; not fitting with what surrounds it
words.ex: A tuxedo looks incongruous at a beach party.
words.ety: in- (not) + congruous (fitting together harmoniously).

words.d: to confirm or support with additional evidence
words.ex: Two witnesses corroborated her account.
words.ety: Latin, to strengthen.

words.d: to decorate; to add details, sometimes untrue, to make a story more interesting
words.ex: He embellished the story every time he told it.
words.ety: Old French, to make beautiful; Latin bellus, pretty.

words.d: greedy for wealth
words.ex: The avaricious landlord raised the rent again.

words.d: quick and superficial; done without attention to detail
words.ex: He gave the contract only a cursory glance.
words.ety: Latin currere, to run — also course, curriculum, courier. Nothing to do with cursing.

words.d: mild (of weather); merciful and lenient (of people)
words.ex: We hoped for clement weather on the wedding day.
words.ety: Latin clemens, mild.

words.d: producing a lot of money; profitable
words.ex: She left teaching for a lucrative job in sales.
words.ety: Latin lucrum, gain — also lucre (money, as in Shakespeare's 'filthy lucre').

words.d: to set aside or assign for a particular purpose
words.ex: The city allocated funds for a new library.

words.d: a model of excellence; a perfect example
words.ex: The Gettysburg Address is a paragon of concise speechwriting.

words.d: similar in some respects, so that a comparison can be made
words.ex: The heart is analogous to a pump.

words.d: daily; also active in the daytime
words.ex: Squirrels are diurnal; owls are nocturnal.
words.ety: Latin diurnus, of a day.

words.d: a false reason given to hide the real one
words.ex: He used a family emergency as a pretext to leave early.
words.ety: Latin praetextum, literally something woven in front — a front or cover.

words.d: to pay or help pay the cost of
words.ex: The grant will defray part of the travel expenses.

words.d: brief and to the point; sometimes curt
words.ex: He sent a terse reply: 'Not interested.'

words.d: a timely blessing or benefit
words.ex: The new bus line has been a boon to commuters.
words.ety: Once meant a favor asked of a king or queen ('grant me this boon'); that sense is now archaic.

words.d: the working class, especially industrial wage earners
words.ex: Marx predicted the proletariat would overthrow the owners of capital.
words.ety: Latin proletarius, a Roman citizen of the lowest class.

words.d: made up of different or unrelated kinds; mixed
words.ex: The city has a wonderfully heterogeneous population.
words.ety: Greek hetero- (other, different), as in heterodox. Its opposite uses homo- (same): homogeneous, homogenize, homonym.

words.d: a very small amount, especially of money
words.ex: He worked all summer for a pittance.

words.d: speaking smoothly and easily, but too smoothly to be sincere or thoughtful
words.ex: The glib salesman had an answer for everything.

words.d: a strong liking or inclination
words.ex: She has a penchant for spicy food.

words.d: to limit or confine; literally, to draw a line around
words.ex: Her role was tightly circumscribed by the contract.
words.ety: Latin circum (around) + scribere (to write, draw). The same circum- gives circumstance, circumvent (get around), circumnavigate and circumlocution (roundabout talk).

words.d: trying to win favor by flattery or charm, usually insincerely
words.ex: He flashed his ingratiating smile at the boss again.
words.ety: Latin in (into) + gratia (grace): getting into someone's good graces.

words.d: motivated only by money; a soldier hired to fight for pay
words.ex: His interest in the charity was purely mercenary.

words.d: to speak or perform without preparation; to improvise
words.ex: When the slides failed, she extemporized for ten minutes.

words.d: severe or stern; strictly simple, without comfort or ornament
words.ex: The monks lived in austere cells with a bed and a chair.

words.d: to make a bad situation better or more bearable
words.ex: New housing programs aim to ameliorate conditions for the poor.

words.d: to erase completely, as if it had never existed
words.ex: The judge ordered the conviction expunged from his record.

words.d: a minor weakness or flaw in character
words.ex: His only foible is a fondness for terrible puns.
words.ety: Originally the weaker part of a sword blade; related to feeble.

words.d: showing intense, passionate feeling
words.ex: She is a fervent supporter of public libraries.
words.ety: Latin fervere, to boil, glow — also behind fervid.

words.d: to draw out or prolong, especially needlessly
words.ex: The lawyers protracted the trial for months.
words.ety: Latin trahere/tractare, to draw, drag.

words.d: showy and designed to impress; flashy
words.ex: They threw an ostentatious party with ice sculptures and fireworks.

words.d: a state of perplexity or uncertainty about what to do
words.ex: She was in a quandary over which offer to accept.

words.d: to criticize sternly or reprimand formally; strong official disapproval
words.ex: The Senate voted to censure the member for misconduct.

words.d: to raise petty, unnecessary objections
words.ex: Critics caviled about the font while ignoring the book's ideas.

words.d: to absorb and incorporate (ideas, food, people) so they become part of the whole
words.ex: Immigrant families often assimilate within a generation. She assimilated the new rules quickly.
words.ety: Latin ad (to) + similis (like): to make like.

words.d: to cancel, repeal or take back
words.ex: The company rescinded the job offer.
words.ety: Latin, to cut back or away.

words.d: able to be perceived or detected
words.ex: There was no discernible difference between the copies.
words.ety: Latin discernere, to sift apart, distinguish.

words.d: a violent upheaval or disaster; originally a great flood
words.ex: The war was a cataclysm that reshaped Europe.
words.ety: Greek, to wash away. Disaster = 'bad star'; catastrophe = 'a down-turning' (the tragic final turn of a Greek play); debacle = a violent breakup of river ice, hence a collapse; calamity = a deeply personal misfortune.

words.d: excessive self-love and self-admiration
words.ex: His narcissism made it impossible for him to listen to others.
words.ety: From Narcissus, the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection.

words.d: to make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing
words.ex: The emails incriminated two senior managers.

words.d: a mark of shame or disgrace
words.ex: The stigma of mental illness keeps many from seeking help.
words.ety: Greek, a mark or brand, as burned into slaves and criminals.

words.d: shortness of time; conciseness of expression
words.ex: Brevity is the soul of wit.
words.ety: Latin brevis, short — also brief, and breve, the little curve over a vowel marking a short sound.

words.d: extremely poor; needy
words.ex: The clinic offers free care to indigent patients.

words.d: able to perceive things beyond normal senses; unusually perceptive; a person with that power
words.ex: You don't need to be clairvoyant to see the merger coming.
words.ety: French, from Latin clarus (clear) + videre (to see).

words.d: skillful and clever, with the hands or the mind
words.ex: She was adroit at steering the meeting away from trouble.
words.ety: French à droit, 'to the right': English has always favored the right hand. Latin dexter (right) gives dexterous and ambidextrous; Latin sinister (left) came to mean evil; French gauche (left) means socially awkward.

words.d: a dull, overused remark delivered as if it were profound
words.ex: His speech was a string of platitudes about teamwork.
words.ety: French plat, flat: a flat remark.

words.d: a long, bitter feud, especially a blood feud between families
words.ex: The two families carried on a vendetta for three generations.
words.ety: Italian, from Latin vindicta, vengeance — also behind vindictive.

words.d: clear and easy to understand; also mentally clear and rational
words.ex: She gave a lucid explanation of the tax changes.
words.ety: Latin lux, light.

words.d: most noticeable or important; projecting outward
words.ex: Let me summarize the salient points of the report.
words.ety: Latin salire, to leap: something that leaps out at you.

words.d: absolute and unconditional; with no exceptions
words.ex: The minister issued a categorical denial.
words.ety: In logic, a categorical statement affirms without conditions; Kant's categorical imperative is an unconditional moral law.

words.d: impossible to understand or interpret; mysterious
words.ex: His motives remain inscrutable.
words.ety: in- (not) + Latin scrutari (to examine) — also scrutinize and scrutiny.

words.d: to interpret or understand in a particular way
words.ex: Her silence was construed as consent.
words.ety: Same Latin source as construct; a 'construction' can also mean an interpretation.

words.d: to refer to something indirectly
words.ex: He alluded to 'recent difficulties' without explaining them.

words.d: providing for future needs; thrifty
words.ex: A provident couple, they saved from their first paycheck.
words.ety: Same Latin root as provide: to prepare for what is coming.

words.d: to attribute something, usually a fault, to someone
words.ex: Critics impute the decline in sales to poor management.

words.d: shrewd and perceptive; quick to see what is to one's advantage
words.ex: An astute investor, she sold before the crash.

words.d: a mystery; a person or thing hard to understand
words.ex: Her sudden resignation remains an enigma.

words.d: belief or acceptance that something is true
words.ex: Don't give credence to gossip. His calm manner lent credence to his story.
words.ety: Latin credere, to believe — like creed, credible and credulous.

words.d: to regard with deep, almost religious respect
words.ex: The villagers venerate the old shrine.

words.d: excessively talkative, especially about trivial things
words.ex: A garrulous passenger talked through the entire flight.
words.ety: Latin garrire, to chatter — Garrulus is also the genus name of chattering jays.

words.d: independent and self-governing
words.ex: The region became an autonomous province.
words.ety: Greek autos (self) + nomos (law): self-ruling. Auto- also gives autobiography, autograph, automatic and autocracy (rule by one person).

words.d: lasting a very short time
words.ex: Internet fame is often ephemeral.
words.ety: Greek, lasting only a day. Journalism shares the idea (French jour, day), which makes 'daily journal' redundant.

words.d: burdensome and hard to bear
words.ex: The new reporting rules are onerous for small firms.
words.ety: Latin onus, a burden — still used in English: 'the onus is on you'.

words.d: lay people as opposed to clergy; non-specialists as opposed to professionals
words.ex: Medical jargon confuses the laity.

words.d: sharp to taste or smell; sharply biting in expression
words.ex: The pungent smell of garlic filled the kitchen. Her pungent humor stung.
words.ety: Latin pungere, to prick — also behind poignant and expunge.

words.d: a fake who claims knowledge or skill he doesn't have
words.ex: The 'healer' turned out to be a charlatan.

words.d: done routinely, with little interest or care
words.ex: He gave a perfunctory nod and went back to his phone.
words.ety: Latin, to get through, be done with.

words.d: a swamp; figuratively, a confusing, entangling situation
words.ex: The project sank into a morass of paperwork.

words.d: clever but deceptive reasoning
words.ex: The lawyer's argument was pure sophistry.
words.ety: Greek sophos, wise (as in sophisticated). The ancient Sophists taught rhetoric for pay and became notorious for slippery arguments.

words.d: producing abundantly — offspring, fruit or works
words.ex: Agatha Christie was a prolific writer.
words.ety: Latin proles, offspring.

words.d: of this world, earthly; commonly, ordinary and dull
words.ex: Monks set aside mundane concerns. She was bored by mundane chores.
words.ety: Latin mundus, world.

words.d: a person who disagrees openly with an established authority; dissenting
words.ex: Dissidents were jailed for criticizing the regime.
words.ety: Latin dis (apart) + sedere (to sit): to sit apart.

words.d: deserving praise
words.ex: Her efforts to help the homeless are laudable.
words.ety: Latin laudare, to praise — also laud and laudatory.

words.d: impossible to imitate; matchless
words.ex: She told the story in her own inimitable style.
words.ety: in- (not) + imitable. The prefix in- can mean 'in' (inhale, ingress) or 'not' (informal, inaudible).

words.d: worn out or dulled, especially by too much of something
words.ex: Jaded by years of luxury, he found nothing exciting anymore.
words.ety: A jade was a worn-out horse, a nag.

words.d: nearsighted; figuratively, lacking foresight or a broad view
words.ex: Cutting research to save money is a myopic decision.

words.d: able to be proved or shown; obvious
words.ex: The new drug has demonstrable benefits.

words.d: to agree or give in quietly, without protest but often with reservations
words.ex: Despite her doubts, she acquiesced to the plan.

words.d: harmful, especially to health or well-being
words.ex: Smoking has deleterious effects on the lungs.
words.ety: Greek, destructive.

words.d: deeply, often sadly or dreamily, thoughtful
words.ex: He sat by the window in a pensive mood.
words.ety: French penser, to think; Latin pensare, to weigh.

words.d: done without preparation; spontaneous
words.ex: The best man gave an impromptu speech.
words.ety: Latin in promptu, in readiness, at hand.

words.d: an educated guess based on incomplete evidence; to make one
words.ex: The cause of the fire is still a matter of conjecture.
words.ety: Latin con- (together) + iacere (to throw): to throw together an opinion.

words.d: so good it serves as an example; commendable
words.ex: Her exemplary service earned her a promotion.

words.d: flawless; incapable of doing wrong
words.ex: He has impeccable taste in clothes.
words.ety: in- (not) + Latin peccare (to sin): unable to sin. Relatives: peccadillo (a small sin), peccant (guilty). Before b, m and p, in- becomes im-; before l, il-; before r, ir- (imbalance, immutable, illogical, irreproachable).

words.d: to confirm or bear witness that something is true; to be evidence of
words.ex: Several colleagues attested to her honesty. The ruins attest the city's former glory.
words.ety: Latin ad + testari, to bear witness (testis, a witness) — also testify, testimony, testator and intestate (without a will).

words.d: abundant; plentiful
words.ex: She took copious notes in every lecture.
words.ety: Latin copia, plenty — as in cornucopia, the horn of plenty.

words.d: based on false reasoning; misleading
words.ex: The argument rests on a fallacious assumption.

words.d: an accusation made in return; a countercharge
words.ex: The meeting dissolved into bitter recriminations.
words.ety: re- (back) + Latin criminari (to accuse): to accuse in return.

words.d: a natural liking or attraction; a close resemblance or relationship
words.ex: She has an affinity for jazz. There's a clear affinity between Spanish and Italian.
words.ety: Latin, relationship by marriage.

words.d: liable to change suddenly and unpredictably; explosive; (chemistry) quick to evaporate
words.ex: The situation in the region is volatile.
words.ety: Latin volare, to fly — every sense suggests flying off into another state. Cousin: volant, able to fly.

words.d: filthy and wretched from poverty or neglect; morally degraded
words.ex: The workers lived in squalid barracks.
words.ety: Latin squalere, to be rough, dirty, neglected.

words.d: to speed up a process or action
words.ex: Paying the extra fee will expedite your passport application.
words.ety: Latin expedire, to free the feet (from a snare).

words.d: utterly wretched and hopeless; lacking all self-respect
words.ex: They lived in abject poverty. He offered an abject apology.
words.ety: Latin ab (away) + iacere (to throw): cast off.

words.d: talking easily, rapidly and at length
words.ex: The voluble tour guide never paused for breath.

words.d: to express sympathy; to share someone's sorrow
words.ex: Her coworkers commiserated with her when she lost the account.
words.ety: Latin, to pity: by derivation, to share someone's misery.

words.d: a situation requiring a choice between two equally undesirable options
words.ex: He faced the dilemma of betraying a friend or lying to the court.
words.ety: Greek di- (two) + lemma (proposition).

words.d: lasting only a short time; by nature bound to pass
words.ex: Fame is transitory.
words.ety: Latin transire, to go across — also transit and transition.

words.d: generous in helping others, especially through large donations
words.ex: The foundation funds philanthropic work around the world.
words.ety: Greek philein (to love) + anthropos (human being): loving humankind. Compare philosophy, philharmonic, anthropology.

words.d: sluggishness and lack of energy; drowsy dullness
words.ex: A heavy lunch always left him in a state of lethargy.

words.d: eager to fight or argue; combative
words.ex: The pugnacious senator picked a fight with every reporter.
words.ety: Latin pugnare, to fight with fists — also pugilist, a boxer.

words.d: deep, sincere remorse for wrongdoing
words.ex: He expressed genuine contrition and offered to repay everything.
words.ety: Latin, a crushing: crushed by guilt.

words.d: hard to manage or control; stubborn
words.ex: The intractable dispute dragged on for years.
words.ety: in- (not) + Latin tractare (to handle) — as in traction and tractor.

words.d: unselfish concern for the welfare of others
words.ex: She volunteers out of pure altruism.

words.d: an award, praise or mark of honor
words.ex: The film won accolades from critics around the world.
words.ety: Latin ad (to) + collum (neck): originally the embrace and sword-tap on the shoulders that conferred knighthood. Also AK-uh-lahd and other variants.

words.d: the pupa stage of a butterfly in its case; a sheltered, undeveloped stage
words.ex: She emerged from the chrysalis of college ready for the world.

words.d: refined and polite, often affectedly so
words.ex: They lived in genteel poverty, keeping up appearances.
words.ety: French gentil, noble, polite.

words.d: cheerful, good-humored and jolly
words.ex: The jovial host greeted everyone with a joke.
words.ety: From Jove (Jupiter), the merry, feast-loving chief Roman god — 'by Jove!'

words.d: a trick or deception used to hide a motive or escape something
words.ex: They got into the party by subterfuge.
words.ety: Latin, to flee secretly.

words.d: bubbling enthusiasm and high spirits
words.ex: She couldn't contain her ebullience after the win.
words.ety: Latin ebullire, to boil up, bubble.

words.d: not allowing anything to pass through; not affected by
words.ex: The jacket is impervious to rain. He seems impervious to criticism.

words.d: to protest or object forcefully
words.ex: She remonstrated with the manager about the unfair schedule.

words.d: to erase or wipe out; to make oneself inconspicuous
words.ex: Time had effaced the inscription on the stone.

words.d: a fanciful, impossible idea; (myth) a monster with a lion's head, goat's body and serpent's tail
words.ex: Total job security is a chimera.

words.d: incapable of being corrected or reformed; unruly
words.ex: He's an incorrigible practical joker.
words.ety: in- (not) + corrigible (capable of being corrected).

words.d: to place side by side, especially for comparison or contrast
words.ex: The exhibition juxtaposes old photos with new ones of the same streets.
words.ety: Latin iuxta (next to) + ponere (to place) — also position.

words.d: familiar with and knowledgeable about
words.ex: She is conversant with several programming languages.
words.ety: Latin conversari, to associate with — also converse and conversation.

words.d: favorable; promising success
words.ex: The company made an auspicious start, selling out in a week.
words.ety: Latin auspex, a Roman who foretold the future by watching birds (avis, bird + specere, to look). Under the auspices of = with the backing of.

words.d: traveling from place to place, especially for work
words.ex: Itinerant farmworkers follow the harvest north.

words.d: to select and gather from many sources; to remove inferior ones from a group
words.ex: She culled the best quotes from hundreds of interviews.
words.ety: Latin colligere, to gather — also collect.

words.d: to announce officially; to make widely known
words.ex: The ministry promulgated new safety rules.

words.d: a system of names used in a science or field
words.ex: Botanical nomenclature uses two Latin names for each plant.
words.ety: Latin nomen (name) + calare (to call). A Roman nomenclator whispered voters' names to candidates.

words.d: amusing in an odd, dry or whimsical way
words.ex: He has a droll sense of humor.

words.d: impossible to satisfy
words.ex: She has an insatiable curiosity.
words.ety: Latin satis, enough — also satisfy, satiate and satiety (fullness to excess).

words.d: to charm or captivate; also to deceive by trickery
words.ex: The serpent beguiled Eve. Her stories beguiled the children for hours.
words.ety: be- (thoroughly) + guile (crafty deceit). Be- also intensifies besmirch, befuddle and beware.

words.d: having or showing a strong desire for revenge
words.ex: His vindictive ex-partner tried to ruin his reputation.
words.ety: Latin vindicta, vengeance (see vendetta).

words.d: fully supplied; abundantly filled
words.ex: The museum is replete with Renaissance art.
words.ety: Latin replere, to fill again — plenus (full) gives plenty, plenitude and plenary (complete: a plenary session).

words.d: to prevent from happening; to make impossible in advance
words.ex: His injury precluded any chance of playing in the final.
words.ety: Latin prae (before) + claudere (to shut): to shut the door beforehand.

words.d: informal; used in ordinary conversation rather than formal writing
words.ex: 'Gonna' is a colloquial form of 'going to'.
words.ety: Latin colloquium, conversation (com- together + loqui to speak).

words.d: friendly, lively and fond of feasting and good company
words.ex: The dinner had a convivial atmosphere.
words.ety: Latin convivium, a feast (con- together + vivere to live).

words.d: to deliberately avoid or abstain from
words.ex: She eschews social media.

words.d: remarkably great in size, extent or degree; amazing
words.ex: He has a prodigious memory for faces.
words.ety: Latin prodigium, an omen or marvel — also prodigy.

words.d: formal approval or praise
words.ex: The plan won the approbation of the board.

words.d: sleight of hand; any clever trickery or deception
words.ex: The accountant's financial legerdemain fooled auditors for years.
words.ety: Middle French léger de main, light of hand.

words.d: partnership or involvement in wrongdoing
words.ex: He denied any complicity in the fraud.
words.ety: Latin complicare, to fold together — also complicate and accomplice.

words.d: to change completely in form, nature or substance, usually for the better
words.ex: Alchemists tried to transmute lead into gold.
words.ety: Latin trans (across) + mutare (to change).

words.d: to instruct and improve morally or intellectually
words.ex: The documentary both entertained and edified.

words.d: deep, full and rich in sound
words.ex: The actor's sonorous voice filled the theater.

words.d: to warn or reprove gently but earnestly
words.ex: She admonished him to slow down before he burned out.
words.ety: Latin admonere, to remind, warn.

words.d: a typical example, model or pattern
words.ex: Her company became the paradigm for ethical sourcing.

words.d: roundabout; indirect
words.ex: We took a circuitous route to avoid the traffic.
words.ety: From circuit, a route that goes around and comes back.

words.d: to clear of blame or suspicion by proving it unjustified; to justify
words.ex: The new evidence vindicated her.

words.d: to exclude from a group or society
words.ex: After the scandal, his colleagues ostracized him.
words.ety: Ancient Athenians voted to banish a citizen by writing his name on a potsherd (ostrakon). In Syracuse they used olive leaves — petalism.

words.d: an excess; an overabundance
words.ex: The report contains a plethora of dull statistics.
words.ety: Greek plethein, to be full.

words.d: a natural tendency, usually toward something bad
words.ex: He has a proclivity for exaggeration.
words.ety: Latin, a sloping forward.

words.d: corresponding in size, amount or degree; proportionate
words.ex: She wants a salary commensurate with her experience.
words.ety: Latin, measured together.

words.d: continuing without pause; unceasing
words.ex: The incessant barking kept us awake.
words.ety: in- (not) + Latin cessare (to cease).

words.d: only slightly related; digressing from the main subject
words.ex: His comments were tangential to the debate.
words.ety: From tangent, a line that touches a curve without crossing it; to go off on a tangent.

words.d: able to be defended or upheld
words.ex: Her argument is no longer tenable in light of the new data.
words.ety: Latin tenere, to hold — also tenacious.

words.d: unable to be felt by touch; hard to grasp with the mind
words.ex: An impalpable sense of dread hung over the house.
words.ety: im- (not) + palpable (Latin palpare, to touch gently). Doctors palpate, examine by touch.

words.d: hateful; deserving or causing strong dislike
words.ex: He had the odious habit of taking credit for others' work.
words.ety: Latin odium, hatred — English odium means hatred or disgrace incurred.

words.d: seeming to be everywhere at once
words.ex: Smartphones are now ubiquitous.
words.ety: Latin ubique, everywhere.

words.d: to think deeply and at length; to mull over
words.ex: She ruminated on the offer all weekend.
words.ety: Latin ruminare, to chew the cud. Ruminants (cows, sheep, camels) re-chew food from the first stomach, the rumen.

words.d: payment for work or services
words.ex: The remuneration barely covered his expenses.

words.d: a small, easily forgiven sin or fault
words.ex: Arriving five minutes late is a peccadillo, not a crime.
words.ety: Spanish, from Latin peccare, to sin (see impeccable).

words.d: lying on the back, face up; also passive and inactive
words.ex: The patient lay supine on the table.

words.d: holding opinions that differ from accepted beliefs
words.ex: His heterodox views on economics annoyed his colleagues.
words.ety: Greek hetero- (other) + doxa (opinion). Ortho- means right or correct: orthodox, orthodontics, orthography (correct spelling), orthoepy (correct pronunciation).

words.d: using pompous, lofty language
words.ex: The mayor's grandiloquent speech said very little.
words.ety: Latin grandis + loqui (to speak). Relatives: magniloquent (pompous), breviloquent (brief), suaviloquent (smooth), somniloquent (talking in one's sleep).

words.d: mournful, often exaggeratedly or comically so
words.ex: The basset hound gave a lugubrious howl.
words.ety: Latin lugere, to mourn.

words.d: too small to be measured
words.ex: The chance of winning is infinitesimal.

words.d: to provoke or urge someone into action; a pointed stick for driving cattle
words.ex: His friends goaded him into jumping.

words.d: to state positively and confidently
words.ex: She averred that she had never seen the man.

words.d: a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds
words.ex: A cacophony of car horns filled the street.
words.ety: Greek kakos (bad) + phone (sound). Caco- also gives cacography (bad writing), cacology (bad word choice), cacoepy (bad pronunciation) and cacoethes (an incurable itch or bad habit).

words.d: stubbornly disobedient; resistant to control, heat or treatment
words.ex: A refractory mule. A refractory case of eczema.

words.d: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
words.ex: An iconoclast in the art world, she mocked every sacred cow.
words.ety: Greek, an image breaker — originally someone who smashed religious images.

words.d: to weaken; to drain of energy
words.ex: The heat enervated the runners.

words.d: lightness of manner, especially when out of place
words.ex: This is no time for levity.
words.ety: Latin levis, light — also levitate.

words.d: calmness and evenness of temper, especially under stress
words.ex: She accepted the news with equanimity.
words.ety: Latin aequus (even) + animus (mind).

words.d: a severe criticism; also a restriction, or a narrowing of a body passage
words.ex: He ignored the critic's strictures.
words.ety: Latin stringere, to draw tight — also strict and stringent.

words.d: very wealthy; luxurious and showy
words.ex: They lived in an opulent mansion.
words.ety: Latin opulentus, rich, linked to Ops, Roman goddess of the harvest.

words.d: to belittle; to speak of as inferior
words.ex: Don't disparage your rivals in public.
words.ety: Old French, to marry beneath one's rank (Latin par, equal — as in peer and on a par).

words.d: deviating from what is normal or expected; irregular
words.ex: This year's sales figures are anomalous.
words.ety: Greek, not the same.

words.d: to shorten by cutting off a part, often severely
words.ex: The editor truncated the article to half its length.
words.ety: Latin truncare, to maim; truncus, a tree trunk with the branches lopped off.

words.d: moderate in eating and drinking; self-denying
words.ex: An abstemious eater, she skipped dessert every night.
words.ety: Latin abstemius, abstaining from wine.

words.d: extremely light, delicate and heavenly
words.ex: The choir's ethereal voices filled the cathedral.
words.ety: From ether, the airy element the ancients believed filled the heavens.

words.d: pompous and inflated in language, with little substance
words.ex: His bombastic speech promised everything and explained nothing.
words.ety: Bombast was once cotton padding for clothes — now verbal padding.

words.d: growing old; declining with age
words.ex: The town's senescent industries were closing one by one.
words.ety: Latin senex, old — also senile and senate (a council of elders).

words.d: universal; broad-minded and wide-ranging in interests or tastes
words.ex: She has catholic taste in music, from opera to hip-hop.
words.ety: Greek katholikos, universal. Lowercase catholic has nothing to do with religion.

words.d: a harsh rebuke; a vehement scolding
words.ex: He endured his father's objurgation in silence.
words.ety: Latin ob (against) + iurgare (to scold).

words.d: a change of circumstances, usually unwelcome; the ups and downs
words.ex: The company survived the vicissitudes of twenty turbulent years.

words.d: quarrelsome; likely to provoke argument
words.ex: Immigration is a contentious issue.
words.ety: Latin contendere, to strive against — also contend and contention.

words.d: a gesture or attitude of deep respect, like a bow
words.ex: The courtiers made obeisance to the queen.
words.ety: French, obedience.

words.d: diligent, persistent and careful
words.ex: Her assiduous research turned up the missing letters.
words.ety: Latin assiduus, sitting down to a task (sedere, to sit — also sedentary).

words.d: deceitful double-dealing
words.ex: The spy's duplicity went undetected for years.
words.ety: Latin duplex, double: doubleness of heart or speech.

words.d: a loyal follower who carries out orders without question or scruple
words.ex: The dictator's myrmidons rounded up his critics.
words.ety: The Myrmidons were the fierce warriors who followed Achilles to Troy.

words.d: to give in or agree to, often under pressure; to take office
words.ex: The union refused to accede to the company's demands.
words.ety: Latin accedere, to come near.

words.d: youth or immaturity; legally, the period of being a minor
words.ex: In his nonage he could not sign a contract.
words.ety: Anglo-French non + age: not of age.

words.d: a crafty scheme or plot with a sinister purpose
words.ex: When his machinations were exposed, he was demoted to the mail room.
words.ety: Latin machinari, to contrive; machina, device — also machine and deus ex machina.

words.d: easy to teach or manage; submissive
words.ex: The docile pony let the children ride all afternoon.
words.ety: Latin docilis, teachable; docere, to teach — also docent and doctrine.

words.d: formidable; arousing fear and respect
words.ex: Small airlines faced redoubtable competition from the big carriers.
words.ety: Old French redouter, to dread; Latin dubitare, to doubt — also dubious.

words.d: to predict, especially from signs or present indications
words.ex: Pundits prognosticate the outcome of every election.
words.ety: Greek prognosis, knowing beforehand.

words.d: to bring about; give rise to
words.ex: An exchange of invective between nations can engender war.
words.ety: Latin generare, to beget — originally meant to procreate.

words.d: stinking; foul-smelling, as of rot or decay
words.ex: A fetid odor rose from the swamp.
words.ety: Latin fetere, to stink.

words.d: to surrender, especially on agreed terms
words.ex: After a month of siege, the garrison capitulated.
words.ety: Latin caput, head: to draw up terms under headings — compare decapitate.

words.d: a person who represents, advocates or explains an idea
words.ex: Carrie Nation was a fierce exponent of temperance.
words.ety: Latin exponere, to put forth — also expound.

words.d: lying; untruthful
words.ex: The mendacious salesman swore the car had never been in an accident.
words.ety: Latin mendax, lying.

words.d: loud, harsh and grating; shrill
words.ex: Her strident voice cut through the noise of the market.
words.ety: Latin stridere, to make a harsh noise — also stridor and stridulate (to chirp, as crickets do).

words.d: government by a few powerful people
words.ex: A small oligarchy of landowners ran the island.
words.ety: Greek oligos (few) + archein (to rule).

words.d: shining brightly; radiant
words.ex: She gave him a refulgent smile.
words.ety: Latin re- (back) + fulgere (to shine).

words.d: favoritism shown to relatives, especially in jobs
words.ex: Promoting his niece to office manager was flagrant nepotism.
words.ety: Italian nepote, nephew; Latin nepos — coined for popes who enriched their 'nephews'.

words.d: humorous in a coarse, mildly indecent way
words.ex: The sailors sang ribald songs below deck.
words.ety: Old French ribauld, a wanton person.

words.d: to beg humbly and earnestly
words.ex: The prisoners supplicated the king for mercy.
words.ety: Latin supplicare, to kneel; supplex, on bended knee — also supple.

words.d: relentless; impossible to stop or move by pleading
words.ex: Joe pleaded for an extra day off, but his manager was inexorable.
words.ety: Latin inexorabilis, not moved by entreaty.

words.d: an upstart who has suddenly gained wealth or power but isn't accepted by the class he joined
words.ex: The old families snubbed the parvenu and his gold-plated yacht.
words.ety: French parvenir, to arrive or succeed: one newly arrived.

words.d: obvious, deliberate exaggeration for emphasis
words.ex: 'I've told you a million times' is hyperbole.
words.ety: Greek hyperbole, a throwing beyond; overshooting the mark.

words.d: making a hypocritical show of piety or moral superiority
words.ex: His sanctimonious lectures on thrift ended when we saw his new car.
words.ety: Latin sanctimonia, holiness; sanctus, holy.

words.d: to prevent a difficulty by anticipating it; make unnecessary
words.ex: A timely phone call obviated the need for a meeting.
words.ety: Latin obviare, to meet in the way; obvius, in the way — also obvious.

words.d: pay or profit from employment or office
words.ex: Make sure the emolument is commensurate with your experience.
words.ety: Latin emolumentum, the miller's fee for grinding grain; emolere, to grind out.

words.d: refusing to compromise or give ground
words.ex: Both sides were intransigent, and the talks collapsed.
words.ety: Latin in- (not) + transigere (to come to a settlement).

words.d: shrewd and wise, especially in practical matters
words.ex: A sagacious lawyer asks only questions she knows the answers to.
words.ety: Latin sagax, keen-scented — first used of hunting dogs quick to pick up a scent.

words.d: sour or bitter; harsh in tone or temper
words.ex: His acerbic reviews made him feared in the theater world.
words.ety: Latin acerbus, bitter like unripe fruit.

words.d: marked with patches of different colors; varied
words.ex: The variegated leaves were streaked with cream and green.

words.d: help in time of distress; to give such help
words.ex: Volunteers gave succor to the homeless on Thanksgiving.
words.ety: Latin succurrere, to run to help.

words.d: to make less severe; gloss over or excuse
words.ex: The press agent tried to palliate her role in the scandal.
words.ety: Latin palliare, to cloak; pallium, a cloak.

words.d: a correction or improvement, especially to a text
words.ex: The editor's emendations restored the poem's original wording.

words.d: to remove objectionable material from a text
words.ex: The school board expurgated the textbook.
words.ety: Latin expurgare, to cleanse — also purge and pure.

words.d: a morally abandoned person; thoroughly wicked
words.ex: The old reprobate cheated even his own brother.
words.ety: Latin reprobare, to disapprove strongly. In theology, one rejected by God.

words.d: the power of choosing; free will
words.ex: She came of her own volition.
words.ety: Latin volo, I will.

words.d: to insert something, especially words into a text or remarks into a conversation
words.ex: Someone had interpolated a forged paragraph into the will.
words.ety: Latin interpolare, to refurbish, alter.

words.d: to cite as evidence or proof
words.ex: The lawyer adduced three precedents to support her case.
words.ety: Latin adducere, to lead to, bring forward.

words.d: to fester; form or discharge pus
words.ex: Left untreated, the wound began to suppurate.

words.d: a strict disciplinarian; a stickler for rules
words.ex: The new manager was a martinet about lunch breaks.
words.ety: From Jean Martinet, a harsh 17th-century French drillmaster.

words.d: a twinge of guilt or regret
words.ex: She quit the job without compunction.
words.ety: Latin compungere, to prick — conscience pricking. Also puncture, pungent, poignant.

words.d: a quack remedy; a dubious scheme for solving social problems
words.ex: Every candidate had a nostrum for the economy.
words.ety: Latin noster, our: the quack's 'our own remedy'.

words.d: the power to produce the desired effect
words.ex: Trials proved the efficacy of the new drug.

words.d: equivalent in effect or meaning
words.ex: Your silence is tantamount to a confession.
words.ety: Anglo-French tant amunter, to amount to as much.

words.d: an outcast; someone shunned by society
words.ex: After the scandal he became a pariah in Hollywood.
words.ety: Tamil paraiyar, a low caste in India.

words.d: closely relevant to the subject at hand
words.ex: The judge ruled the remarks not germane to the case.
words.ety: Latin germanus, having the same parents — closely related.

words.d: lacking moral restraint, especially sexually
words.ex: The novel was banned for its licentious scenes.
words.ety: Latin licentia, freedom — also license.

words.d: too old to be useful; outdated or retired
words.ex: They finally scrapped the superannuated computer system.
words.ety: Latin super (beyond) + annus (year).

words.d: conspicuously bad; flagrant
words.ex: It was an egregious error to send the email to the whole company.
words.ety: Latin egregius, standing out from the herd — once meant outstanding in a good way.

words.d: an odd, stubbornly held notion or whim
words.ex: Using a fountain pen was one of his crotchets.
words.ety: Middle English crochet, a hook — a notion that hooks you.

words.d: an inscription on a building; a quotation at the start of a book or chapter
words.ex: The novel's epigraph came from Ecclesiastes.
words.ety: Greek epi (on) + graphein (to write).

words.d: to speak or write at great length; elaborate
words.ex: He expatiated on the history of the parish for an hour.
words.ety: Latin exspatiari, to wander.

words.d: a paid position requiring little or no work
words.ex: His uncle found him a sinecure on the harbor board.
words.ety: Latin sine cura, without care — a church post with no care of souls.

words.d: a natural preference or liking
words.ex: She has a predilection for Italian cuisine.

words.d: waste parts of a butchered animal; refuse
words.ex: Gulls fought over the offal from the fish market.
words.ety: Middle English off + fall: what falls off.

words.d: slender, supple and graceful
words.ex: The lissome dancer leapt across the stage.

words.d: sweetly flowing, like honey (of sounds or words)
words.ex: The narrator's mellifluous voice made the audiobook a pleasure.
words.ety: Latin mel (honey) + fluere (to flow).

words.d: to overfeed or oversupply; an excess
words.ex: We were surfeited with turkey. There's a surfeit of apartments on the market.
words.ety: Old French sorfait, excess.

words.d: flattering or coaxing words or actions
words.ex: She resisted the salesman's blandishments.
words.ety: Latin blandiri, to flatter, caress — also bland.

words.d: tediously long-winded; wordy
words.ex: The prolix report ran to three hundred pages.
words.ety: Latin prolixus, extended.

words.d: greed, especially for money or possessions
words.ex: The scheme preyed on the cupidity of its investors.
words.ety: Latin cupiditas, desire — also Cupid. But cupidity means love of money, not romance.

words.d: of or like spring; fresh and youthful
words.ex: The vernal equinox falls in March.
words.ety: Latin ver, spring.

words.d: a re-establishing of friendly relations
words.ex: The summit marked a rapprochement between the two rivals.
words.ety: French rapprocher, to bring together again. Keeps its French pronunciation.

words.d: a long, formal discussion or essay on a subject
words.ex: She delivered a disquisition on Byzantine coinage.

words.d: to forbid or outlaw
words.ex: The ordinance proscribes the sale of fireworks.
words.ety: Latin proscribere, to post an outlaw's name.

words.d: lavish generosity
words.ex: Thanks to the donor's munificence, the library got a new wing.
words.ety: Latin munus (gift) + facere (to make).

words.d: complete honesty and integrity, proven under test
words.ex: Her probity made her the obvious choice for treasurer.
words.ety: Latin probus, good, upright.

words.d: powerful; mighty
words.ex: The puissant empire stretched from sea to sea.
words.ety: Old French, powerful.

words.d: to embezzle, especially public or entrusted funds
words.ex: The treasurer peculated thousands from the pension fund.
words.ety: Latin peculium, private property.

words.d: extremely stingy
words.ex: The parsimonious landlord refused to fix the heater.

words.d: flashy and falsely attractive; tawdry
words.ex: The novel's meretricious plot twists couldn't hide its emptiness.
words.ety: Latin meretrix, a prostitute.

words.d: an urgent need or situation demanding immediate action
words.ex: The exigencies of war required rationing.
words.ety: Latin exigere, to demand.

words.d: the final unraveling of a plot; the outcome of a complex situation
words.ex: In the denouement, the long-lost twin returns.
words.ety: French dénouer, to untie, as a knot.

words.d: fleeting; passing quickly
words.ex: Fame on social media is fugacious.
words.ety: Latin fugere, to flee — also fugitive.

words.d: impossible to annul, undo or take away
words.ex: Once the mortgage was paid, she held indefeasible title.
words.ety: Anglo-French defesable, able to be undone.

words.d: insincere; pretending to be candid when you aren't
words.ex: It was disingenuous of him to claim he'd never heard of the plan.
words.ety: Latin ingenuus, freeborn, noble, frank.

words.d: coarsely abusive; vulgar and defamatory
words.ex: The pamphlet made scurrilous attacks on the senator.
words.ety: Latin scurra, a buffoon or jester.

words.d: a fresh outbreak after a period of quiet
words.ex: Analysts feared a recrudescence of inflation.
words.ety: Latin recrudescere, to become raw again — of a wound reopening.

words.d: to throw out of a window
words.ex: In 1618, Protestant nobles defenestrated two officials in Prague.
words.ety: Latin de- (out of) + fenestra (window).

words.d: causing delay; slow and tardy
words.ex: The senator's dilatory tactics stalled the bill.
words.ety: Latin dilator, a delayer.

words.d: acquired by chance; not inherent
words.ex: The research turned up some adventitious discoveries.
words.ety: Latin adventicius, coming from outside — also advent.

words.d: thoroughly dried; figuratively, lifeless
words.ex: Desiccated coconut lasts for months. His desiccated prose put readers to sleep.
words.ety: Latin desiccare, to dry up completely.

words.d: courtesy and mutual respect, especially between nations
words.ex: The treaty rested on the comity of nations.
words.ety: Latin comitas, courteousness.

words.d: to criticize harshly; literally, to strip off the skin
words.ex: The review excoriated the director for wasting a fine cast.
words.ety: Latin excoriare, to strip off the hide (corium, hide).

words.d: weariness; listless exhaustion
words.ex: A heavy lunch brought on an afternoon of lassitude.
words.ety: Latin lassus, weary.

words.d: to disgrace by spreading lies; slander publicly
words.ex: The tabloid traduced the senator with fabricated quotes.
words.ety: Latin traducere, to lead across — parade someone in disgrace.

words.d: shamefully wicked; villainous
words.ex: The Holocaust was one of history's most flagitious crimes.
words.ety: Latin flagitium, a shameful crime.

words.d: walking or traveling from place to place; one who does
words.ex: A peripatetic salesman, he lived out of his car.
words.ety: Greek, walking about: Aristotle taught while strolling in the Lyceum, so his followers were the Peripatetics.

words.d: to laugh loudly and uncontrollably
words.ex: The audience cachinnated at the comedian's punch line.
words.ety: Latin cachinnare, to laugh aloud.

words.d: atonement for a wrong; the act of making amends
words.ex: He spent his retirement in expiation of the harm he had done.
words.ety: Latin expiare, to atone (pius, devout).

words.d: dull and insubstantial; lacking interest or nourishment
words.ex: The film's jejune dialogue bored even the critics.
words.ety: Latin ieiunus, fasting, empty — also jejunum, the part of the small intestine found empty after death.

words.d: a serious scarcity or lack
words.ex: A paucity of funds ended the project.
words.ety: Latin paucus, few.

words.d: threatening; menacing
words.ex: Minatory clouds gathered over the hills.
words.ety: Latin minari, to threaten — also menace.

words.d: commonly supposed or reputed, but not proven
words.ex: The putative father demanded a DNA test.
words.ety: Latin putare, to think, suppose.

words.d: laborious study, especially late at night; a learned, often overwrought piece of writing
words.ex: Years of lucubration produced a ten-volume history.
words.ety: Latin lucubrare, to work by lamplight (lux, light).

words.d: a cave dweller; a primitive, brutish or reclusive person
words.ex: His coworkers were troglodytes who had never opened a novel.
words.ety: Greek, one who creeps into holes.

words.d: depending on chance or luck
words.ex: Day trading is an aleatory business.
words.ety: Latin aleator, a dice player; alea, a game of dice.

words.d: a confused mixture; a jumble
words.ex: His speech was a farrago of half-truths and clichés.
words.ety: Latin farrago, mixed fodder for cattle.

words.d: the center of attention or admiration
words.ex: The bride was the cynosure of every eye.
words.ety: Greek kynosoura, dog's tail — the Little Dipper, whose tip is the North Star, a sailor's guide.

words.d: priestly; used by priests; sacred
words.ex: The priests performed hieratic rites in the temple.
words.ety: Greek hieros, sacred — also hierarchy and hieroglyphic.

words.d: to spoil or impair; corrupt morally; make legally invalid
words.ex: One false entry vitiated the whole contract.
words.ety: Latin vitium, fault, vice.

words.d: laughable; provoking laughter
words.ex: His risible excuse fooled no one.
words.ety: Latin ridere, to laugh — also ridicule and ridiculous.

words.d: to treat as a celebrity
words.ex: Hollywood lionized the young director after her first hit.
words.ety: From lion, a famous or fascinating person: a literary lion.

words.d: an awkward, embarrassing mishap
words.ex: There was a contretemps when the speaker's slides wouldn't load.
words.ety: French, against the time — originally a badly timed thrust in fencing.

words.d: boastful, blustering talk
words.ex: Behind the rodomontade, the general had no plan.
words.ety: From Rodomonte, a boastful king in Italian Renaissance epics.

words.d: mental dullness; lethargy
words.ex: The long meeting left everyone in a state of hebetude.
words.ety: Latin hebes, blunt, dull.

words.d: cheerfully confident; optimistic
words.ex: She was sanguine about the company's prospects.
words.ety: Latin sanguis, blood: blood was the humor of a cheerful, ruddy temperament.

words.d: a skilled conversationalist at the dinner table
words.ex: A good dinner party needs at least one deipnosophist.
words.ety: Greek deipnon (meal) + sophistes (wise man), after Athenaeus's Deipnosophistae, learned men talking at dinner.

words.d: breakable; easily damaged
words.ex: Even steel is frangible when struck by another car.
words.ety: Latin frangere, to break — also fragile and fracture.

words.d: clearly proven; beyond dispute
words.ex: The proof was apodictic: no one could find a flaw.
words.ety: Greek apodeiktikos, demonstrative.

words.d: to criticize cuttingly; literally, to scratch or make small cuts in the skin or soil
words.ex: The review scarified the young author.
words.ety: Greek skariphos, a stylus. Unrelated to scare.

words.d: weekly
words.ex: The club held hebdomadal meetings every Thursday.
words.ety: Greek hebdomas, a group of seven.

words.d: to wander; digress
words.ex: His lecture divagated from Napoleon to his own childhood.
words.ety: Latin dis- (apart) + vagari (to wander) — also vague and vagabond.

words.d: caused by medical treatment
words.ex: The rash was iatrogenic, a reaction to the antibiotic.
words.ety: Greek iatros (healer) + -genic (caused by).

words.d: desertion of a cause or faith; evasive shifting and equivocating
words.ex: After years of tergiversation, the senator finally switched parties.
words.ety: Latin tergum (back) + versare (to turn): to turn one's back.

words.d: pearly; like mother-of-pearl
words.ex: The shell's nacreous lining shimmered pink and green.
words.ety: From nacre, mother-of-pearl.

words.d: an idler; lazy and good for nothing
words.ex: Her faineant son refused to look for work.
words.ety: French fait-néant, does nothing.

words.d: covered with stiff, bristly hairs
words.ex: The caterpillar's hispid back stung his fingers.
words.ety: Latin hispidus, shaggy, bristly.

words.d: long-suffering patience under hardship
words.ex: She bore her long illness with remarkable longanimity.
words.ety: Latin longus (long) + animus (spirit).

words.d: a person with only superficial knowledge who pretends to know more
words.ex: The sciolist bluffed his way through the wine tasting.
words.ety: Latin sciolus, a smatterer; scire, to know.

words.d: nearness in place, time or relationship
words.ex: Propinquity, more than passion, explains many office romances.
words.ety: Latin propinquus, near.

words.d: complicated and intricate, like a network
words.ex: The novel's plexiform plot required a chart of characters.
words.ety: From plexus (a network of nerves or vessels) + form.

words.d: a soft whispering or rustling sound
words.ex: A susurrus passed through the audience as the lights dimmed.
words.ety: Latin susurrare, to whisper.

words.d: to grind into a fine powder
words.ex: The pharmacist triturated the tablets with a mortar and pestle.
words.ety: Latin triturare, to thresh, grind.

words.d: to crackle, snap or pop
words.ex: Logs crepitated in the fireplace.
words.ety: Latin crepitare, to crackle — also decrepit (with creaking bones).

words.d: wandering at night
words.ex: Owls and noctivagant revelers had the streets to themselves.
words.ety: Latin nox (night) + vagari (to wander) — also vague, vagabond, vagary.

words.d: sooty or smoky; figuratively, murky and obscure
words.ex: They met in a fuliginous back room of the bar.
words.ety: Latin fuligo, soot.

words.d: urging or encouraging; giving earnest advice
words.ex: The coach's hortatory halftime speech fired up the team.
words.ety: Latin hortari, to urge — also exhort.

words.d: sun worship
words.ex: Every summer the beach fills with devotees of heliolatry.
words.ety: Greek helios (sun) + latreia (worship).

words.d: shadowboxing; fighting an imaginary enemy
words.ex: The debate was sciamachy: each side attacked positions no one held.
words.ety: Greek skia (shadow) + mache (battle).

words.d: smooth and hairless
words.ex: The cactus is glabrous, unlike its fuzzy cousin.
words.ety: Latin glaber, bald, smooth.

words.d: a petty, tricky, unscrupulous lawyer
words.ex: The pettifogger dragged out the case over a $40 fence.

words.d: having characteristics of both sexes, or of neither; sexless
words.ex: The model's epicene look blurred the line between menswear and womenswear.
words.ety: Greek epikoinos, common to both.

roots.m: belief, doctrine / one who does or believes
